title: ACLU of Texas, Partners Again Urge U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit To Give Texas ...
description:
The petition requests the Fifth Circuit to reconsider a divided panel decision that upheld a decision to invalidate the Texas Dream Act.
The Dream Act enabled a generation of Texans to grow their careers and become leaders in our communities.
The consent judgment ended the Texas Dream Act and circumvented the will of the Texas Legislature.
On June 24, 2025, the ACLU of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, Democracy Forward, National Immigration Law Center, and Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann filed a motion to intervene.
The district court denied their motion, and they appealed to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.
text:
AUSTIN, TX — The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, Democracy Forward, National Immigration Law Center, and the Dallas-based firm of Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann today filed a petition for rehearing en banc at the Fifth Circuit today on behalf of La Unión del Pueblo Entero (LUPE), the Austin Community College District’s Board of Trustees (ACC), and graduate student Oscar Silva. The petition requests the Fifth Circuit to reconsider a divided panel decision that upheld a decision to invalidate the Texas Dream Act.

On June 4, 2025, the Department of Justice (DOJ) sued the State of Texas to block the Texas Dream Act, an in-state college tuition law passed with bipartisan support in 2001. The Dream Act guaranteed access to in-state tuition and financial aid for persons (including non-citizens, permanent residents, and visa holders) who meet certain eligibility requirements, including graduating from and completing at least three years in Texas high schools. The Dream Act enabled a generation of Texans to grow their careers and become leaders in our communities.

However, just six hours after the DOJ filed the lawsuit—and without time for impacted individuals to defend the Dream Act—Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton entered into a consent judgment with the federal government. The consent judgment ended the Texas Dream Act and circumvented the will of the Texas Legislature.

This has created sweeping uncertainty for impacted students, colleges, and universities.

On June 24, 2025, the ACLU of Texas, Texas Civil Rights Project, Democracy Forward, National Immigration Law Center, and Lynn Pinker Hurst & Schwegmann filed a motion to intervene. The motion asked that the district court allow LUPE, ACC, and Oscar to challenge this abusive litigation strategy and to defend the constitutionality of the Texas Dream Act. The district court denied their motion, and they appealed to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.

In July 2026, in a 2-1 divided panel decision, the Fifth Circuit Federal Court of Appeals denied the appeal, leaving the district court/lower court ruling enjoining the state law in place. The en banc petition asks the entire Fifth Circuit to review the case. The petition also highlights the exceptional importance of the legal issues at stake, including using the court system to end a decades-old law increasing education access across the state.

“Texas is stronger when every young person, regardless of citizenship status, has the opportunity to learn and reach their full potential,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the Texas Civil Rights Project. “Texas’ in-state tuition law was in effect for more than two decades, and the Texas Civil Rights Project will continue to fight to ensure it is restored for future generations of Texans. We are proud to stand with Texas Dreamers and fight back against the federal government’s vicious sue and settle strategy, which clearly aimed to reject the will of the people by overturning a law that was upheld across every state legislative session since its inception.”

“By challenging this collusive litigation, we are not only fighting to restore a decades-old law that has allowed tens of thousands of students to thrive, but we are also continuing to fight for the right of every individual, regardless of their immigration status, to pursue an accessible and affordable higher education,” said Kassandra Gonzalez, senior attorney at the Texas Civil Rights Project.

Abbott has refused to sign a rendition warrant that would pave the way for the officer to return to Minnesota for trial.

text:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) asserted to a judge Monday that he’s not obligated to hand over an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged by Minnesota authorities with shooting a Venezuelan man earlier this year during “Operation Metro Surge.”

Minnesota is pushing in court to force the extradition of ICE officer Christian Castro, with a key hearing slated for Tuesday. The state insists Abbott has no discretion to avoid signing the warrant.

“In the end, Minnesota’s zeal to see Mr. Castro prosecuted on its home turf cannot justify pretermitting Governor Abbott’s ongoing deliberations pursuant to the Constitution and state statutes, which are designed to protect against abusive and baseless deprivations of individual liberty,” Abbott’s lawyers wrote in their formal written response to the court.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr., an appointee of President Trump who oversees the case, will consider Minnesota’s bid at a Tuesday afternoon hearing in his Brownsville, Texas, courtroom.

It has become a major legal clash between Abbott and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D), who requested Castro’s extradition as state authorities charged the ICE officer with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

The officer stands accused of injuring a Venezuelan man in the leg by firing a gun at the front door of an occupied Minneapolis home on Jan. 14 amid an immigration enforcement surge in the Twin Cities. Castro had allegedly told investigators he opened fire in self-defense after being hit with a shovel and a broom, only for video footage to undercut the officer’s claim.

Abbott has refused to sign a rendition warrant that would pave the way for the officer to return to Minnesota for trial.

In the new filing, the governor’s lawyers raised doubts that Castro qualifies for the Constitution’s extradition requirement. It demands a state return defendants facing criminal charges who “flee from Justice” when they are “found in another State.” Abbott has suggested Castro didn’t flee because ICE had ordered him to return to Texas.

“The ordinary meaning of a fugitive entails a volitional act of fleeing, not mere involuntary movement across state lines,” his lawyers wrote.

Minnesota insists that Abbott’s role is ministerial, and the state wants a judge to immediately pave the way for the officer to be returned.

“The Framers of the Constitution and Congress intended the interstate extradition process to be a swift, summary one in which the state into which a defendant travels promptly returns a fugitive as soon as the requesting state demands it,” the state wrote in court filings last week.

Abbott cautioned he hasn’t yet made a final decision on the extradition request. But his new filing said that any notion Minnesota could unilaterally enforce the extradition power was “doomed to fail.” His filing also took shots at Walz for pardoning a man charged with sexually assaulting a minor.

“Equity favors those with clean hands,” Abbott’s lawyers wrote.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Marc Rosenblum, the first-ever leader of the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Homeland Security Statistics, this week rejoined the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) as a visiting senior fellow.

Rosenblum, who earlier was an MPI senior policy analyst and later deputy director of its U.S. Immigration Policy Program, has nearly three decades of bipartisan experience in the executive and legislative branches, the research community and academia in immigration policy and data collection and analysis.

He brings to MPI his extensive experience building the data capabilities of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) through four administrations (beginning with the Obama administration and continuing through the first Trump, Biden and first 18 months of the second Trump terms), as well as policy knowledge gained during prior work at the Congressional Research Service (CRS), in the Senate and as a tenured professor.

“We are delighted to welcome Marc back to MPI, where he will be a key voice as we continue our work developing and proposing ideas for improving the U.S. immigration system,” said Doris Meissner, who directs MPI’s U.S. Immigration Policy Program.

Said MPI President Andrew Selee: “Marc’s experiences in and out of government and across administrations of both political parties also give him a unique vantage point in continuing the work he and MPI have long championed to make essential immigration-related data accessible to the public.”

Under Rosenblum, the DHS Office of Immigration Statistics grew into the Office of Homeland Security Statistics (OHSS), with expanded data collection, reporting and analysis across the department, including its immigration components: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

Rosenblum is also joining More in Common as a senior fellow, where he will advise on its immigration public opinion research.

Prior to his DHS, MPI and CRS stints, Rosenblum served as a Council on Foreign Relations international affairs fellow detailed to the office of Senator Edward Kennedy, where he contributed to Senate immigration legislative efforts in 2006 and 2007. From 2011-2013, he served on the National Research Council's Committee on Estimating Costs of Immigration Enforcement in the Department of Justice.

Rosenblum is widely published and is co-editor (with Daniel Tichenor) of The Oxford Handbook of International Migration (Oxford University Press).

He holds a B.A. from Columbia University and a Ph.D. from the University of California, San Diego. He began his career as an assistant and then associate professor of political science at the University of New Orleans.

text:
CEUTA, Spain (AP) — Against the murmur of prayers, body bags were lowered into graves marked only with numbers. Gravediggers placed the first four victims in cinderblock plots while a small group of locals watched at a cemetery on the tip of North Africa.

The dead, whose identities are unknown, were among the more than 90 migrants who lost their lives during Spain’s deadliest border crisis three weeks ago. Fueled by misinformation, poverty and a lack of opportunities, more than 72,000 people poured into Ceuta, a Spanish territory that neighbors Morocco.

At a Muslim cemetery in Ceuta, 18 migrants were laid to rest on Friday. An Islamic cleric read prayers and chants praising God while funeral workers worked quickly to lower the white body bags and cover them with soil. More migrants are expected to be buried soon.

The Moroccan Association for Human Rights, a left-leaning nongovernmental organization, called for the burials in Ceuta to be halted until every effort had been made to identify the bodies and repatriate them to Morocco, the country of origin for most of the migrants who made the perilous journey.

Many of those who died drowned or were killed in a stampede to cross a breakwater barrier near a border checkpoint.

In a statement, the NGO asked Morocco’s foreign ministry to ensure that “the bodies are returned to the families so they can be buried with dignity.”

It called the burials in Ceuta a “new human tragedy,” adding to the “disaster of displacement and missing persons.”

A spokesperson for Ceuta’s city government said last week the paperwork to repatriate the bodies of the deceased was complete, but that Morocco’s government hadn’t accepted it.

Morocco’s foreign ministry didn’t respond to questions from The Associated Press about the burials that started on Friday in Ceuta or suggestions that Morocco is blocking the repatriation of identified migrant bodies.

While most of those who crossed into Ceuta in late July returned to Morocco almost immediately, local authorities say that up to 10,000 migrants — including women and children — could still be in the small Spanish city, prolonging a humanitarian crisis as authorities and locals struggle to shelter and attend to them. Spain’s national government cites a lower figure of around 5,000 people.

Moroccan and Spanish authorities have blamed social media rumors and human smuggling networks for the deadly event, while migrants cited unemployment and low wages as reasons for why they made the journey.

All of those buried on Friday were men, said Said Mohammed, the cemetery’s acting manager. The graves were marked with numbered stones in case families claim the bodies in the future, he said.

Under Islamic custom, a body is placed in a grave facing Mecca, as was the case with the migrants buried in Ceuta. Just across the sea lay mainland Europe — their desired destination.

___

Suman Naishadham reported from Madrid. Akram Oubachir contributed to this report from Casablanca, Morocco.

The original proposal applied to universities, hospitals and research-based institutions; however, those employers won’t be impacted by the new fee under the DHS’s newly proposed rule.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a new proposed rule for H-1B visas on Monday that would charge a $103,265 fee for all workers seeking to gain employment in the U.S. who are subject to the annual statutory cap.

Notice of the proposed rule says the fee would be used for the federal government’s costs of administering the lawful immigration system, including activities carried out by the DHS and the departments of Justice, State and Labor.

“The proposed H‑1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers,” U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a release.

The move follows a federal judge’s decision in June to strike down the Trump administration’s previously proposed $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications.

U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin ruled that it was unlawful to implement a tax on visa applications, as Congress is the only legislative body with the authority to set immigration policy and taxes.

The original proposal applied to universities, hospitals and research-based institutions; however, those employers won’t be impacted by the new fee under the DHS’s newly proposed rule.

“The administration claims the new fee will be a ‘cost recovery mechanism,’ even though the first fee led to a nearly 90 percent reduction in filings and a $28 million loss in revenue. The government itself told the court that the $100,000 fee was ‘arguably prohibitive’ and ‘does not raise revenue,'” David Bier of the Cato Institute said in a statement sent to The Hill.

“Even if it did raise revenue, that would not make it legal because immigration fees can only be imposed to recover the costs of adjudication and naturalization services. And because this is a filing fee, employers would have to pay it with no guarantee that USCIS [U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services] will approve the petition. Almost no one will risk more than $100,000 with no guarantee of approval,” Bier added.

The standard annual statutory limit for new H-1B visas is 85,000, which comprises the regular cap of 65,000 visas and 20,000 visas granted to applicants who hold a master’s degree or higher from a U.S. college or university. Out of the 65,000, a total of 6,800 are set aside exclusively for Chilean and Singaporean nationals.

The tech industry has been at the center of discussions surrounding H-1B visas, which allow U.S. companies to hire foreign workers in specialized, high-skill occupations.

Computer-related positions make up nearly two-thirds of all H-1B approvals, focusing heavily on software engineering, data science and IT support, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.

Companies and tech workers will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule once it’s published on the Federal Register, which officials say will happen Tuesday.

Updated 4:23 p.m. EDT

text:
Just last week, Georgia Rep. Nikema Williams, along with several members of Congress, visited the immigration detention facility in Lumpkin, Georgia. Williams described what she saw as “cruel” and “inhumane” for the people who were detained there.

The congresswoman also stated that immigration agents did not want the lawmakers there and allegedly did not want to answer any questions, “even though they’re required to by law.” Representatives with three human and civil rights groups say they’re experiencing the same stonewalling from federal immigration officials.

“If members of Congress have difficulty accessing these types of facilities, imagine how difficult it is for family members of people who have loved ones detained there to get answers about their families,” said Samantha Hamilton, senior litigation staff attorney at Asian Americans Advancing Justice – Atlanta. “It can be really difficult for family members, even attorneys who represent people detained in places like Stewart, places like Irwin, places like the Folkestone ICE Processing Center to get even the most basic information about the welfare of their clients, of their loved ones, about the medical issues that they might be facing inside.”

According to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, Georgia remains among the top five states with the most immigration detainees, with more than 4,500 people in custody. That total is up 90% since President Donald Trump returned to the White House, as the AJC reported.

AAAJ-Atlanta, along with the ACLU of Georgia and Project South, have now filed a federal lawsuit, instructing ICE to follow through on a Freedom of Information Act request. The organizations are seeking information on plans to expand immigration detention in Georgia. They also want further details on the use of the Atlanta ICE Field Office to detain immigrants.

“Earlier this year in March, our three organizations had sent a letter to ICE regarding the conditions, particularly in what we call the hold cell, which is some cells in the basement of the field office in Atlanta, not a detention center,” said staff attorney Raneem Ashrawi with the ACLU of Georgia. “Reports were coming out of there in regard to how long people were held there and the conditions in which they were being held.”

Although they tried to get more insight into what was happening inside the Atlanta facility and what changes have been made, Ashrawi said immigration officials are not willing to let them visit and see things for themselves.

Hamilton, Ashrawi, and Project South’s senior staff attorney Priyanka Bhatt discussed their legal action on Monday’s “Closer Look with Rose Scott.” Bhatt said it is “appalling that ICE is going to such lengths to hide the truth” about the inhumane conditions inside the Atlanta ICE Field Office holding cells.

“We are super concerned with the conditions inside these ICE detention centers and holding facilities,” Bhatt said. “And the public have a right to know, and that’s exactly why we’re filing this lawsuit.”

text:
Colorado administers a universal preschool program (UPK) that offers free preschool for four-year-olds statewide. Private preschools that participate in the voluntary program—whether secular or religious—receive taxpayer funds to cover the costs of educating these students. To participate, eligible preschools must abide by the state program’s nondiscrimination policy, which requires that preschools not discriminate against either children or parents based on, among other traits, sexual orientation or gender identity. This requirement applies to all preschools participating in Colorado’s UPK program, and there is no pathway for any preschool to be exempted from the program’s ban on discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Two Catholic parishes that run (or ran) a preschool filed suit, along with the Archdiocese of Denver and two parents with preschool-age children. They argued that Colorado’s refusal to exempt them from the UPK program’s nondiscrimination policy violates the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause by excluding preschools and families from receiving state benefits because of their religion. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit upheld the Colorado program. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, and CAC filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of First Amendment scholars in support of Colorado.

Our brief makes two principal points. First, it argues that Founding-era history regarding the free exercise of religion does not support the petitioners’ claim that they are entitled to an exemption from a neutral and generally applicable civil law. Several Founding-era state constitutions included provisions that protected the free exercise of religion but also made clear that individuals were not permitted to violate the peace and safety of other citizens in the exercise of their religion. Further, Founding-era congressional debates support the view that the Free Exercise Clause was not understood to have conferred a broad religious exemption from compliance with civil laws.

Second, the brief explains why ruling for petitioners would require the Court to depart from decades of precedent, including Employment Division v. Smith and cases both before and after it. Pre-Smith precedent made clear that the government has both a compelling interest in eradicating discrimination and broad authority to conduct its internal affairs without conforming to every individual’s religious views. Smith itself held that where “prohibiting or burdening the free exercise of religion ‘is not the object [of a law] but merely the incidental effect of a generally applicable and otherwise valid provision, the First Amendment has not been offended.’” And no case since Smith has suggested that neutral and generally applicable policies like Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement must yield to requests for religious exemptions. Under the Court’s precedents, when “followers of a particular sect enter into commercial activity as a matter of choice”—like running a preschool that seeks to join Colorado’s UPK program—“the limits they accept on their own conduct as a matter of conscience and faith are not to be superimposed on the statutory schemes which are binding on others in that activity.” Taken together, this body of precedent leads to the conclusion that the petitioners have no right to participate in voluntary state-funded programs without complying with the government’s nondiscrimination policy for all participants.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a new $103,265 filing fee for all H-1B cap-subject petitions.

Proposes Permanent $100,000 Fee for H-1B Cap-Subject Petitions

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) that would establish a new $103,265 filing fee for all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including petitions eligible for the advanced degree exemption. The proposed fee would be imposed in addition to all existing H-1B filing fees and would be payable at the time of filing

According to DHS, the proposed fee is intended to generate revenue to support the costs of administering the U.S. legal immigration system across multiple federal agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), the Department of State (DOS) and the Department of Labor (DOL).

Who Would Be Impacted?

If finalized, the rule would apply to:

All H-1B cap-subject petitions

Petitions filed under the annual 65,000 H-1B cap

Petitions filed under the 20,000 advanced degree exemption

The proposal would not apply to cap-exempt H-1B petitions, including many petitions filed by higher education institutions, affiliated nonprofit entities, nonprofit research organizations and governmental research organizations.

Proposed Fee Separate from Ongoing $100,000 H-1B Litigation

DHS states that the proposed $103,265 fee is based on a separate statutory authority from the administration’s 2025 presidential proclamation that imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain H-1B petitions. That earlier policy remains the subject of ongoing litigation.

Notably, DHS indicates that if the proclamation ultimately survives legal challenges or is extended, employers could potentially be required to pay both amounts.

“To the extent a petitioner is subject both to a proclamation-required payment and to the additional H-1B fee proposed in this rule, the petitioner would be required to pay both amounts.”

Why Is DHS Proposing the Fee?

According to the NPRM, DHS determined that current immigration fees do not generate sufficient revenue to fund the full cost of administering the lawful immigration system. The agency considered increasing fees across all immigration benefit requests but instead decided to allocate those costs specifically to H-1B cap-subject employers.

How was the $103,265 Fee Calculated?

DHS calculated the proposed fee by dividing approximately $8.78 billion in annual costs by an estimated 85,000 annual H-1B cap-subject petitions, resulting in a fee of $103,265 per petition.

The agency estimates the fee would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually if all available cap numbers are utilized.

Where Would the Revenue Go?

Under the proposal, DHS would distribute revenue generated by the fee among several federal agencies involved in immigration administration:

Agency Proposed Annual Allocation USCIS $3.0 billion EOIR (Immigration Courts) $2.96 billion DOL $1.21 billion ICE $1.05 billion DOS $484 million CBP $76.2 million

DHS states that these agencies incur costs related to immigration adjudications, fraud prevention, screening, vetting, immigration court operations, labor condition application processing and other functions supporting the legal immigration system.

Potential Impact on Employers

The proposal would represent one of the most significant fee increases in the history of the H-1B program. Historically, employers generally paid several thousand dollars in filing fees depending on company size and filing circumstances. The new fee would add more than $103,000 to the cost of sponsoring a cap-subject H-1B worker.

DHS acknowledges that the proposal could substantially affect employers, particularly small businesses. According to the agency’s analysis, approximately 11,051 small entities could experience a significant economic impact if the rule is finalized.

Attorney Insight

Peter Bade, Managing Attorney at Corporate Immigration Partners, states:

Given the scope of the proposal and the ongoing litigation surrounding the administration’s previous H-1B fee policy, we expect this rule to face significant legal challenges if DHS moves forward with a final regulation.

It’s also important to remember that this is only a proposed rule.

DHS must first complete the public comment process and determine whether to issue a final regulation, and no implementation date has been announced.

Importantly, the proposed rule is directed at future H-1B cap-subject filings and would not affect petitions that have already been approved. No changes would take effect until DHS ultimately finalizes the rule.

As a result, employers should continue working closely with their immigration counsel and avoid making workforce decisions based on the proposal alone.

What Happens Next?

The proposed rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on August 25, 2026. DHS will accept public comments for 30 days following publication before determining whether to issue a final rule.

Employers that rely on the H-1B program should closely monitor developments, as the proposal could significantly affect future workforce planning, recruitment strategies and immigration sponsorship costs.

text:
While Republican candidates are leaning into harsh anti-immigrant rhetoric and aligning themselves with Trump’s mass deportation campaign to attract voters ahead of November’s midterms, a recent survey shows that most Arizonans prefer an immigration enforcement strategy that emphasizes fair treatment and an easier path to earning citizenship.

The economy and affordability are top of mind for voters, but the shadow of immigration enforcement looms large, following months of aggressive crackdowns across the country and the fatal shootings of two citizens by federal immigration agents in January.

November’s election is expected to be the first political test of the Trump administration’s violent immigration agenda. In Arizona, voters will choose which party will helm the state for the next four years, deciding between candidates who hold starkly different positions on the federal government’s approach to immigration enforcement. And research indicates that hostility to immigrants doesn’t resonate with Arizona voters.

The 2026 Arizona Voters’ Agenda, by the nonpartisan Center for the Future of Arizona, found that an overwhelming majority of voters across the political spectrum want there to be improved access to citizenship for certain immigrants. As much as 86% of voters who are planning to participate in Arizona’s November election, including 75% of Republicans, said the federal government should create a “clearer and easier legal pathway” to citizenship for immigrants who meet established requirements.

Arizona voters also appear to disagree with efforts to expand which immigrants are eligible for removal, a tactic that the Trump administration has increasingly turned to in a bid to raise deportation numbers. Three-fourths of voters in the Grand Canyon State, including 57% of those who identified as Republican, said they support the enforcement of federal immigration laws but emphasized that immigrants already in the country with legal permission should be treated fairly and respectfully.

Few Arizonans said they agreed with strategies that undermine respectful treatment in the name of immigration enforcement. Only 21% of voters reported being comfortable with the possibility of legal immigrants enduring scrutiny or greater restrictions for the sake of implementing federal immigration enforcement goals. Even among Republican respondents, support for enforcement actions that led to the mistreatment of immigrants with legal status was low, at just 36%.

In a written statement, the Center for the Future of Arizona noted that the survey demonstrates that Arizona voters don’t see immigration enforcement or border security as either-or issues.

“Across several major policy questions, they support approaches that combine security, functionality, legal pathways, enforcement, and fair treatment. At the same time, more restrictive alternatives do not earn the same level of agreement across the electorate,” reads the statement.

In November, those priorities may come into play as immigration enforcement and border security are on the ballot in Arizona. Voters will decide whether drug cartels should be labeled terrorist organizations. If passed, Proposition 317 would direct the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to do everything in its power to defend against that threat, and it sets the stage for a future governor to send the National Guard to patrol the state’s southern border.

Arizonans will also pick who will take on the state’s top leadership positions for the next four years, each of which exerts significant influence over how much the state participates in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat who has resisted efforts from the GOP-controlled legislature to facilitate Trump’s mass deportation campaign and prefers instead to award funding grants to border officials, will face off against U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, a vocal proponent of Trump’s agenda who once proposed federal legislation that would have publicized the identities and locations of immigrants with deportation orders, in a bid to turn the public and local law enforcement agents into a national man-hunt.

The race to win the state attorney general’s seat is similarly marked by federal immigration enforcement efforts. Democrat Kris Mayes is hoping voters will award her another term and has touted her lawsuit against Trump’s executive order attempting to end birthright citizenship for the children of immigrants and her support for immigrants who arrived in the country as minors as proof that she is the right choice to represent the state in court.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security’s decision last year to pull additional federal agents for immigration enforcement resulted in a dramatic drop in fentanyl investigations and seizures by the department’s investigations division, according to a federal watchdog report.

The sudden change in approach toward ongoing fentanyl-related efforts stemmed from President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, which required federal agents across the government to be pulled in for immigration arrests. That included agents from Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations, the body charged with combatting cartels and criminal organizations.

Under tremendous pressure to meet White House-imposed quotas, HSI pivoted much of its work in fiscal year 2025 to immigration arrests, pulling it away from some of its ongoing work into fentanyl. One office reported that around “99 percent” of its work was dedicated to immigration, leaving almost no room for fentanyl investigations, according to the DHS inspector general report released last week.

“In FY 2025, Department priorities shifted toward immigration enforcement. Accordingly, HSI prioritized immigration enforcement over fentanyl-related criminal investigations,” the report found.

The report reviewed HSI’s role in disrupting the supply of fentanyl, ranging from the agency’s technologies, coordination with other federal agencies, and shifting priorities. The audit was conducted from March 2025 through May 2026.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, agents had increasingly dedicated time to fentanyl investigations, but in fiscal year 2025, the hours spent on those investigations declined by around 31% compared to the previous fiscal year, the report found.

“At the same time, immigration enforcement saw the largest increase across all investigative categories, rising more than 1.7 million hours (over 800 percent),” the report continued.

That also led to a reduction in fentanyl investigations and seizures. In fiscal year 2025, the number of investigations initiated by HSI dropped by 24% compared to the previous year. At one field office, the number of investigations initiated declined from 30 to 13 from fiscal year 2024 to fiscal year 2025, according to the report.

“HSI’s fentanyl seizures also decreased by 39 percent in FY 2025 despite the DEA reporting several record-breaking fentanyl seizures in 2025,” the report said.

In a statement to CNN, a Homeland Security spokesperson said HSI “is working closely with the Department to track metrics and execute goals to assess how well ICE-HSI is combating fentanyl. In FY26, an action plan was launched as an Agency Priority Goal, which set key milestones for combating fentanyl.”

Agents across HSI offices nationwide reported an all-hands approach to the administration’s immigration push in interviews with the inspector general’s office. For example, one drug investigation team of seven agents was reduced to “two to three” because people were reassigned to immigration cases, the report states.

The audit identified other issues that hamstrung HSI’s efforts to combat fentanyl, including technical limitations, lack of necessary funds, and inconsistent referrals from other federal agencies, like US Customs and Border Protection.

The inspector general shared four recommendations with ICE, which concurred with all of them. That included conducting a review of staffing levels “to ensure an appropriate level of coverage commensurate with the relative priority of fentanyl investigations.” ICE HSI agreed to review staffing and determine next steps, setting an estimated completion date of June 30, 2027.

description:
It’s become a frequent occurrence on highways today, according to Daniel Gonzalez, as the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown extends to foreign-born truck drivers.
This is all part of a bigger effort by the Trump administration to crack down on truck drivers.
DANIEL GONZALEZ: So the Trump administration is focusing on kind of two classes of immigrant truck drivers: truck drivers who are not proficient in English and truck drivers who receive what’s called non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses.
There’s no hard evidence that immigrant truck drivers are any more dangerous than other truck drivers, but nevertheless, that’s who they’re focusing on, and the largest group that are being targeted here are Indian Sikh Punjabi Sikh Indians.
The Trucking Association feels that this kind of influx of truck drivers created a recession in the trucking industry where there was too many truck drivers that drove the price down, and some of these owners are trying to cut costs, and one of the ways they’re doing it is by hiring at lower pay truck drivers who may not be safe to be on the road.
text:
Picture this: A semitruck loaded with 40,000 pounds of frozen chicken worth more than $100,000, abandoned on the side of the Interstate 40.

Why? The driver was arrested and detained by Border Patrol.

It’s become a frequent occurrence on highways today, according to Daniel Gonzalez, as the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown extends to foreign-born truck drivers.

Gonzalez covers immigration for the Arizona Republic.

Full conversation

LAUREN GILGER: Good morning.

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Good morning, nice to be here.

LAUREN GILGER: Thanks for coming in. So these truck drivers are arrested, detained by immigration authorities, then there are these massive loads of goods that are just left on the side of the road. This is all part of a bigger effort by the Trump administration to crack down on truck drivers. It’s called Operation Checkmate. Tell us about that. They say these folks are a danger on the roads essentially.

DANIEL GONZALEZ: So the Trump administration is focusing on kind of two classes of immigrant truck drivers: truck drivers who are not proficient in English and truck drivers who receive what’s called non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses. These are licenses that are issued to people who were born in other countries but live in the United States, and they have legal work permits, and through those legal work permits, they’re able to get a commercial driver’s licenses.

But as part of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, they have been taking away a lot of these work permits from people who are asylum seekers, TPS holders, people like those that are temporarily here, they don’t have actual status, but they have these work permits that allows them to work and get commercial truck drivers licenses.

So when they lose their work permits, they technically are no longer legal to have a commercial driver’s licenses, but often times the driver’s licenses, the expiration date exceeds the work permit dates, so those are the folks that the Trump administration is targeting. And it’s part of this overall mass deportation campaign that’s very much couched in a safety issue.

LAUREN GILGER: Yeah. OK, so the administration basically says this is about safety, right, like you said. That these folks don’t read English or speak English well enough to read the road signs or communicate during an inspection, things like that. Is there any proof of this?

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Well, I think they say that they are finding truck drivers on the roads when they pull them over who do not pass English proficiency tests and therefore should not be driving. But for example, the person that you mentioned in the beginning who had to abandon his load on the side of the I-40 ...

LAUREN GILGER: 40,000 pounds of frozen chicken, yeah.

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Yeah, well I interviewed him. He spoke fluent English extremely well. And so it raises the question of are some of these truck drivers really more that they’re pulling off the road really more about targeting immigrants than boosting the mass deportation campaign.

LAUREN GILGER: They cite some incidents in which there have been accidents involving foreign-born truck drivers, we should say. But when this happens, like you said, you interviewed this person who had to leave their load on the side of the road, the company has to fly someone out to go and drive that load somewhere else. They’re losing a lot of money on this, I’m guessing.

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Yeah, it affects the truck drivers and it affects consumers. In this particular case, he was driving a load of 40,000 pounds of frozen chicken that he had picked up at a processing plant in Indiana, and he was going to deliver it in California at a warehouse.

And on the way on I-40, he was followed by undercover Border Patrol agent, pulled over. He showed him his driver’s license, he showed him his work permit, he told him he had a pending asylum case, his asylum hearing was down the road. They took him, they detained him anyway, and he had to leave his — not only he left his entire rig there and then 40,000 pounds of frozen chicken, and then it took his owner, the owner of the vehicle, five days before he could actually get out to Arizona and pick up that truck.

LAUREN GILGER: So the other criticism here that advocates are pointing out, right, that is that these efforts seem to be aimed specifically at a certain group of immigrant truck drivers: Punjabi Sikh drivers. They wear turbans, practice a certain religion, look a certain way, right?

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Yeah, and going back to the other point that you made, and it fits in with the harassment that critics feel has been unleashed here. So there have been a number of high-profile accidents, and that’s what the Trump administration is using to justify this crackdown, and includes a very horrific accident that took place in the Florida Turnpike back in August of 2025, where an Indian-born truck driver was making a U-turn, he blocked three lanes of traffic, and three people were killed.

And there’s been a number of other spectacular, high-profile accidents like that that have involved immigrant truck drivers. So that’s the justification that the Trump administration is using for this crackdown. There’s no hard evidence that immigrant truck drivers are any more dangerous than other truck drivers, but nevertheless, that’s who they’re focusing on, and the largest group that are being targeted here are Indian Sikh Punjabi Sikh Indians.

And the concern is that this crackdown that has kind of painted Punjabi Sikh or Indian drivers as unsafe has unleashed this wave of harassment. So there’s some legal documents that include details based on interviews with some of these truck drivers that people are throwing water bottles at them, they’re hurling racial slurs at them. So there’s a very ugly aspect that has been unleashed here.

LAUREN GILGER: Yeah. Let me ask you about the other side of this, though, because the Arizona Trucking Association, for example, is happy about this crackdown. They say this is a good thing because of so-called bad actors. What’s their point of view?

DANIEL GONZALEZ: So their point of view is that after the pandemic, there was this huge need for truck drivers, and there was this big influx of foreign-born truck drivers into the trucking industry. And that coincided, as you recall, during the Biden administration where we had millions of asylum seekers crossing the border and making their way into the United States. A lot of those folks who are in the process of applying for asylum or have Temporary Protected Status, they qualify for work permits, and they are able to with these work permits apply for commercial driver’s licenses.

The Trucking Association feels that this kind of influx of truck drivers created a recession in the trucking industry where there was too many truck drivers that drove the price down, and some of these owners are trying to cut costs, and one of the ways they’re doing it is by hiring at lower pay truck drivers who may not be safe to be on the road.

LAUREN GILGER: Right, OK. So let’s talk briefly here in the last minute or so about what’s next. Attorney General Kris Mayes is getting involved. There is a lawsuit sort of pushing back on this crackdown on immigrant truck drivers. What would that do?

DANIEL GONZALEZ: Well, the lawsuit is part of this crackdown. The Trump administration has filed subpoenas to get the records of all these truck drivers that are held in a database that states control.

And the states, Democratic — it should be pointed out — Democratic attorneys general have filed a lawsuit countering that, saying this is an overreach, they’re just going on a fishing expedition, they want to get the personal records of millions of truck drivers to see what they can find out. So they’re fighting that.

LAUREN GILGER: Yeah, OK. Lots to come on this front, I’m sure. Daniel Gonzalez covers immigration for the Arizona Republic, joining us to talk more about this story. Daniel, thank you so much for coming in. Thanks for your reporting here.

text:
A federal agency's refusal to release records related to longstanding immigration fraud allegations involving Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is fueling new questions about whether federal enforcement proceedings could be underway.

News organizations have sought records related to allegations surrounding Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Critics have long alleged the marriage was part of an immigration fraud scheme and have claimed Elmi was Omar's brother.

Omar has denied those allegations, which have not been proven.

According to the response discussed on The National News Desk, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to release requested records under the Freedom of Information Act, commonly known as FOIA, citing concerns that disclosure could interfere with "enforcement proceedings."

Washington insider Armstrong Williams said the language deserves attention but cautioned against treating the exemption itself as proof of wrongdoing.

"The public deserves transparency, but we should not confuse a FOIA exemption with evidence of guilt," Williams said.

Federal agencies can withhold certain law enforcement records under FOIA when releasing them could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings. Such a response does not, by itself, establish that Omar is the subject of an investigation or that the underlying allegations are true.

Asked whether the response could indicate an active federal investigation involving a sitting member of Congress, Williams said those associated with the matters under scrutiny should take the situation seriously, while stopping short of drawing a definitive conclusion.

"I think Omar and anyone associated with her in these programs have cause for great concern," Williams said. "I'll leave it at that."

The controversy comes as Omar continues to face scrutiny from political opponents over her personal history and other matters. She has consistently denied allegations that her marriage to Elmi involved immigration fraud.

The interview then shifted to a separate controversy involving political polling after a 21-year-old college graduate reportedly created a fake polling operation, complete with fabricated results and a website, that was subsequently cited within political and media circles.

Williams said the episode should serve as a warning to journalists, campaigns and voters about accepting polling data without examining how it was produced.

"It is a devastating indictment of the political media ecosystem," Williams said.

"A poll without transparent methodology should never be treated as news," he added.

Williams said legitimate polling can provide valuable information about public opinion, but argued that promoting numbers without verifying the methodology risks influencing voters rather than simply measuring their views.

"When campaigns and journalists promote convenient numbers without verification, and that's what happened, it begins shaping opinions instead," Williams said.

"They're shaping opinions, not news," he added.

The discussion also turned to reports of a private meeting between Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law and former senior White House adviser, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., with the midterm elections approaching.

Williams characterized the meeting as "strategic outreach" and suggested both sides have reasons to maintain lines of communication as control of Congress remains at stake.

"Kushner understands that the Democrats could possibly capture the House, making Jeffries the speaker," Williams said.

A Democratic takeover of the House could significantly alter the balance of power in Washington, potentially giving the party control of congressional committees and investigative authority during the second half of Trump's term.

Williams also argued Jeffries is confronting pressure from the progressive wing of his own party, particularly in New York.

"The meeting expresses both their vulnerability," Williams said.

He suggested the conversation could reflect an effort to identify areas where the Trump White House and Democratic congressional leadership might eventually cooperate if Republicans lose control of the chamber.

"I think they've come to the realization that they have to find a way to cooperate," Williams said, adding that Trump could need to establish a working relationship with Jeffries if he becomes House speaker.

With the midterms little more than two months away, the three developments highlight different uncertainties hanging over Washington: unanswered questions surrounding federal records, renewed skepticism about political polling and behind-the-scenes conversations that could take on greater significance depending on which party controls Congress.

For now, the ICE response does not establish wrongdoing by Omar or confirm that she is personally under federal investigation. But the agency's invocation of an enforcement-related FOIA exemption is likely to keep scrutiny of the longstanding allegations alive as reporters and lawmakers seek additional information.

text:
All US immigration officers working for a key anti-fraud unit have been reassigned by Donald Trump’s administration to focus on screening South African refugees and alleged “unlawful” voters.

Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS) immigration officers have been shifted full-time on to two “high-priority” initiatives, according to internal correspondence seen by the Guardian, leaving US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) unable to provide officers to train asylum officers in “the near future”.

USCIS is inside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has led Trump’s immigration crackdown during his second term. The processing of asylum claims has largely ground to a halt during Trump’s administration, leaving many seeking asylum in limbo.

“All FDNS IOs [immigration officers] have been reassigned full-time to one of two high-priority USCIS initiatives (South African refugee screening and unlawful voter screening),” an internal message, sent on Monday, said. “Because of this, we will not have the ability to assign IO’s [immigration officers] to the training portfolio for the near future.”

USCIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

FDNS is the USCIS unit responsible for detecting fraud and national security concerns in immigration benefit applications, including asylum claims. Its officers work with asylum offices to identify cases requiring further investigation, refer matters to law enforcement, and help asylum officers identify potential fraud and other red flags.

The reassignment marks a significant diversion of FDNS personnel. The message addresses only the agency’s ability to provide officers for asylum officer training; it does not say whether routine FDNS screening of pending asylum applications has also slowed or stopped.

A disruption to training would limit specialized instruction for asylum officers, and a broader slowdown in casework screening would have more direct consequences for pending applications. The Guardian has not independently confirmed whether routine asylum screening has been affected.

The refugee-screening priority is part of the Trump administration’s bid to sharply curtail US refugee resettlement while prioritizing admissions of South Africans, primarily Afrikaners, whom US officials say face racial discrimination and “white genocide”, which the South African government has rejected as unfounded and politically motivated.

The most recent refugee report from the US state department detailed that of the 10,258 refugees admitted to the US between 1 October 2025 and 31 July 2026, 10,255 were from South Africa. The remaining three were Afghans admitted in November.

The second priority identified in the message, screening for “unlawful voters”, appears to be part of a broader administration effort to identify noncitizens alleged to have registered or voted in US elections. Experts have expressed skepticism of the president’s claim that this is a significant problem.

USCIS has already moved to bar naturalization for green card holders who voted or registered to vote, and pursue deportation proceedings against them. A March 2025 executive order opened USCIS’s Save database to state election officials, fueling investigations in several states into noncitizens accused of casting ballots.

Confirmed instances of noncitizen voting have been found to be rare: a February 2026 review by the Center for Election Innovation and Research identified roughly 35 such cases nationwide in the 2024 general election, out of about 154m votes cast.

text:
In Brief

Judge Jeannette Vargas rules visa ban unlawful

Policy affects nationals from 75 countries globally

Visa ban ignores federal anti-discrimination protections

African Communities Together leads lawsuit against policy

The Trump administration must resume processing visas for people from 75 countries that the government deemed likely to become a “public charge,” a federal judge in New York ruled Friday, curbing one of the latest efforts to restrict legal immigration pathways to the United States.

The halt to visa processing began in January, affecting dozens of countries in every corner of the globe. It was meant to limit visas for people the government said would probably rely on public benefits for their basic needs, long a complaint from President Donald Trump.

But U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of President Joe Biden, ruled that the policy “represents a direct abrogation” of consular officers’ exclusive, congressionally granted authority to determine if someone is eligible for a visa.

Vargas also said the nationality-based visa ban, which applied to all nationals of the 75 countries no matter their income or economic status, ignores antidiscrimination protections in federal immigration law.

Vargas’s order came in response to a lawsuit from two nonprofit groups and 11 individuals: six people whose family members’ visa applications had been rejected under the freeze, and another five who had filed work-related petitions to come to the United States.

Amaha Kassa, executive director of African Communities Together, one of the groups that sued, welcomed the ruling against a policy that he said lacked solid evidence or rationale.

“The decision on whether [someone should] receive a visa should be an individual decision,” he said. “It shouldn’t be based on profiling on stereotypes of certain countries.”

A State Department spokesperson declined to comment on ongoing litigation but said in a statement that the Trump administration is “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants.”

The January policy did not affect visas that had already been issued. Nor did it apply to nonimmigrant visas, such as those granted to students and tourists, but otherwise prevented consular officers from issuing visas on work or family grounds.

Experts said that the indefinite pause would turn away nearly half of all legal immigrants over a one-year period. People from the countries affected, many of them in Africa, the Middle East and the Caribbean, account for 40 to 45 percent of all immigrant visas.

The visa freeze followed a broader State Department directive in November that tightened rules around potential immigrants who might become “public charges.”

According to the Associated Press, State Department officials cited data from the Council of Economic Advisers noting that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from the targeted countries received some form of public assistance.

But Kassa, of African Communities Together, said such an approach painted all people from the targeted countries with an overly broad brush. The purpose of these visas, he noted, is often to reunite families.

The visa freeze had been one of many ways in which State Department has sought to restrict migration to the U.S. in recent months.

Also last year, the Trump administration expanded a travel ban on entry to the United States to the citizens of 39 countries after an Afghan immigrant was charged in the shooting of two National Guard troops. Of those countries, 24 were included in the suspension of visa processing.

A federal judge in June ordered the federal government to resume processing citizenship, green-card and work permit applications for people affected by the ban.

text:
A federal agency's refusal to release records related to longstanding immigration fraud allegations involving Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is fueling new questions about whether federal enforcement proceedings could be underway.

News organizations have sought records related to allegations surrounding Omar's 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Critics have long alleged the marriage was part of an immigration fraud scheme and have claimed Elmi was Omar's brother.

Omar has denied those allegations, which have not been proven.

According to the response discussed on The National News Desk, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to release requested records under the Freedom of Information Act, commonly known as FOIA, citing concerns that disclosure could interfere with "enforcement proceedings."

Washington insider Armstrong Williams said the language deserves attention but cautioned against treating the exemption itself as proof of wrongdoing.

"The public deserves transparency, but we should not confuse a FOIA exemption with evidence of guilt," Williams said.

Federal agencies can withhold certain law enforcement records under FOIA when releasing them could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings. Such a response does not, by itself, establish that Omar is the subject of an investigation or that the underlying allegations are true.

Asked whether the response could indicate an active federal investigation involving a sitting member of Congress, Williams said those associated with the matters under scrutiny should take the situation seriously, while stopping short of drawing a definitive conclusion.

"I think Omar and anyone associated with her in these programs have cause for great concern," Williams said. "I'll leave it at that."

The controversy comes as Omar continues to face scrutiny from political opponents over her personal history and other matters. She has consistently denied allegations that her marriage to Elmi involved immigration fraud.

The interview then shifted to a separate controversy involving political polling after a 21-year-old college graduate reportedly created a fake polling operation, complete with fabricated results and a website, that was subsequently cited within political and media circles.

Williams said the episode should serve as a warning to journalists, campaigns and voters about accepting polling data without examining how it was produced.

"It is a devastating indictment of the political media ecosystem," Williams said.

"A poll without transparent methodology should never be treated as news," he added.

Williams said legitimate polling can provide valuable information about public opinion, but argued that promoting numbers without verifying the methodology risks influencing voters rather than simply measuring their views.

"When campaigns and journalists promote convenient numbers without verification, and that's what happened, it begins shaping opinions instead," Williams said.

"They're shaping opinions, not news," he added.

The discussion also turned to reports of a private meeting between Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law and former senior White House adviser, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., with the midterm elections approaching.

Williams characterized the meeting as "strategic outreach" and suggested both sides have reasons to maintain lines of communication as control of Congress remains at stake.

"Kushner understands that the Democrats could possibly capture the House, making Jeffries the speaker," Williams said.

A Democratic takeover of the House could significantly alter the balance of power in Washington, potentially giving the party control of congressional committees and investigative authority during the second half of Trump's term.

Williams also argued Jeffries is confronting pressure from the progressive wing of his own party, particularly in New York.

"The meeting expresses both their vulnerability," Williams said.

He suggested the conversation could reflect an effort to identify areas where the Trump White House and Democratic congressional leadership might eventually cooperate if Republicans lose control of the chamber.

"I think they've come to the realization that they have to find a way to cooperate," Williams said, adding that Trump could need to establish a working relationship with Jeffries if he becomes House speaker.

With the midterms little more than two months away, the three developments highlight different uncertainties hanging over Washington: unanswered questions surrounding federal records, renewed skepticism about political polling and behind-the-scenes conversations that could take on greater significance depending on which party controls Congress.

For now, the ICE response does not establish wrongdoing by Omar or confirm that she is personally under federal investigation. But the agency's invocation of an enforcement-related FOIA exemption is likely to keep scrutiny of the longstanding allegations alive as reporters and lawmakers seek additional information.

text:
NEW ORLEANS—The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University filed an amicus brief on Friday evening in a case seeking to reverse the decision by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) finding Mahmoud Khalil, a lawful permanent resident, deportable. The brief, filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, explains that the evidence uncovered in the Knight Institute’s lawsuit AAUP v. Rubio demonstrates that the government targeted Khalil based on his core political speech as part of a government policy of arresting, detaining, revoking the visas of, and deporting noncitizens who engage in pro-Palestinian advocacy. It also argues that an after-the-fact charge brought against Khalil was a continuation of this effort to punish Khalil and others for their speech. The Knight Institute challenged this policy in federal court, which declared the policy unconstitutional and vacated it earlier this year.

“The Trump administration has used its immigration authority in shocking and unprecedented ways to target Mr. Khalil and other pro-Palestinian advocates based solely on their constitutionally protected speech, and it has done so precisely to terrify others into silence and stifle dissent,” said Xiangnong (George) Wang, staff attorney at the Knight First Amendment Institute. “The court should reverse the BIA’s decision and put an end to Mr. Khalil’s removal proceedings.”

Khalil appealed his immigration case to the Fifth Circuit earlier this month, asking the court to reverse the BIA’s decision finding him removable and to terminate the proceedings entirely. Khalil argued that the BIA lacked the authority to sustain the key ground of his removal, that the grounds for his removal are unconstitutional, and that the immigration judge rushed to a decision without considering relevant evidence, refused to consider the constitutional challenges to his deportation, and improperly sustained pretextual, after-the-fact charges that the Trump administration brought in retaliation for his speech.

In addition to arguing that the government targeted and retaliated against Khalil on the basis of his constitutionally protected political speech, the Knight Institute’s brief agrees with Khalil that the government’s conduct in this case was “outrageous” because Khalil’s advocacy implicates constitutional interests of the highest order, because the government’s targeting of Khalil and others based on their protected speech is particularly egregious, and because Khalil has an undeniable interest is avoiding targeted deportation that outweighs any interest the government may have in removing noncitizens due to disagreement with their views.

The Knight Institute challenged the Trump administration’s deportation policy in March 2025 on behalf of the American Association of University Professors and the Middle East Studies Association. After a nine-day trial, the district court issued a landmark ruling invalidating the Trump administration’s policy of targeting noncitizen students and faculty for arrest, detention, visa revocation, and deportation because of their pro-Palestinian advocacy. The court held that the policy violated the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act and vacated the policy but declined to issue the injunction sought by the plaintiffs. The Knight Institute has asked the First Circuit Court of Appeals to permanently block the policy in order to end its continuing chilling effect on campuses nationwide. Read more about AAUP v. Rubio here.

The Knight Institute also previously filed an amicus brief in Khalil v. Trump, Khalil’s separate challenge to his unlawful arrest and detention, urging the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit to find that the government’s detention and attempted deportation of Khalil on the basis of his protected speech is unconstitutional. Read more about that case here.

Read the Knight Institute’s Fifth Circuit amicus brief here.

Read more about this lawsuit, Khalil v. Blanche, here.

Lawyers on the case include Alex Abdo, Xiangnong (George) Wang, Raya Koreh, and Jameel Jaffer of the Knight First Amendment Institute.

text:
Immigration attorney explains the new H-1B fee proposal.

The Donald Trump administration dropped another H-1B bombshell Monday as it tweaked the $100,000 H-1B fee and issued a draft rule increasing the fee to $103,265. The increase is not the main issue of the new proposal; in the new proposal, every H-1B petition will have to pay this fee, while the earlier $100K was meant for only those who needed to undergo consular processing. This means that the earlier fee was not applicable to those who were already in the US and got selected in the H-1B lottery. But the new proposal says everyone will have to pay the new fee if they are picked by the lottery. Immigration attorney Emily Neumann said it is part of the playbook which believes in throwing enough things at the wall so that something might stick. But this would not stick, Neumann said, explaining that if it becomes final, there will be litigation.

$100k H-1B visa fee

In September 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order bringing in a $100K fee on H-1B visas. The companies were supposed to pay it for every petition they file. Several lawsuits were filed against the fee and it was vacated by the court. As things stand now, for H-1Bs who will join the US workforce from October 1, FY 2027, the companies did not have to pay the fee as courts had blocked the fee. On June 8, 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts ruled that the $100,000 fee requirement was an unlawful tax. : On July 24, 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals formally denied the federal government's request to resume collecting the fee while the appeal proceeds.

$103,265 H-1B visa fee

On August 24, the Department of Homeland Security proposed an increased fee with an expansion of scope. All H-1B workers subject to the annual statutory cap, including those with master's degrees, will come under the new fee. Those who studied in the US, those who already worked in the US would also not be spared from the fee. Neumann said that this time they are using a different statutory authority. "Same number. New wrapper. Same playbook. Throw enough things at the wall to restrict legal immigration and eventually something might stick (this won't). For now, it is only a proposal. Nothing changes yet. And it would apply only to new H-1Bs selected in next year’s cap lottery. There will be a comment period. If it becomes final, there will be litigation," Neumann said.

End of Article

text:
A rights group tracking ICE flights says it’s seeing an uptick in the number of third-country removal flights — a Trump-era process where immigrants are flown from the U.S. to a country other than their own.

Human Rights First produces monthly reports showing all kinds of ICE deportation flights.

During a 24-hour period this month, the group says it tracked several third-country removal flights, including one to Liberia — marking the first time the U.S. has used a new agreement to send people from other countries to the African nation.

“So there was one plane that went to Liberia, and then to Equatorial Guinea and then finally Cameroon, and then at the same time we also saw separate flights to Paraguay, Guatemala and Honduras,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Arvey says many on board had been granted withholding of removal orders by a judge in the U.S. That’s a form of protection that prevents someone from being sent to their home country.

“They’ve already met a high threshold, a higher threshold than asylum, due to the likelihood of persecution or torture in their countries of origin,” she said.

Arvey’s group tracked a plane from Louisiana to Liberia, then to Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon. She says people previously sent to Equatorial Guinea have been sent back to their home countries once they arrive.

As the Arizona Daily Star reported, an Arizona man originally from Egypt is among several people who have been sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they say they’re being held in a decommissioned hotel and subject to abuse by armed guards.

Arvey says 15 people were sent to Liberia, 10 to Cameroon and 12 to Equatorial Guinea.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said the administration is using “all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history.”

The spokesperson did not respond to questions about abuse deportees reported being subjected to in countries where they are sent, and referred questions about the third country agreements to the State Department.

authors: Shelly Brisbin, Texas Standard, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, shelly-brisbin-texas-standard
description:
When migrants who are deaf interact with immigration enforcement officials, they are supposed to have access to a sign language interpreter.
So deaf people under this law are supposed to have access to sign language interpreters when they request them.
There’s another problem that would arise from sign language barriers, and that’s interpreters who can’t sign in the migrant’s language, right?
Yeah, and so this organization called Hands United, which helped deaf immigrants and their families, told me that the U.S. does not recognize certification for sign language interpreters for languages other than American Sign Language.
So interpreters are essentially taken at their word that they can actually interpret in another form of sign language, like Venezuelan Sign Language, Mexican Sign Language.
text:
When migrants who are deaf interact with immigration enforcement officials, they are supposed to have access to a sign language interpreter. But new reporting from Mother Jones has found that some of the more than 100 deaf immigrants who have been deported from the U.S. in 2026 have had no interpreters, or that the service was inadequate to their needs.

Julia Métraux reports on disability issues for Mother Jones. She says migrants have been deported to countries that are not their own, without knowing where they were being sent.

This transcript has been edited lightly for clarity.

Texas Standard: When someone who’s deaf comes in contact with the immigration system, what services are they entitled to receive and what about others with disabilities, too?

Julia Métraux: So under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, any place that receives federal funding is supposed to accommodate the needs of disabled people, and that includes deaf people.

And it’s detention centers and courts where immigration proceedings happen, they both receive federal funding. So deaf people under this law are supposed to have access to sign language interpreters when they request them.

Tell me how this actually plays out in real time. If there’s an immigration enforcement operation, are they supposed to have someone on hand to help a deaf person interact in each of those encounters?

I have to say, just like encounters on the street, I have never heard of a sign language interpreter accompanying ICE agents. Never heard of that happening. I really don’t think it’s happening. But when it comes to being in detention centers, when people are asked to have an interpreter, they’re supposed to get them.

One of the people I spoke to, Emilio, he called Texas home for close to four years. He was prodded to get on a bus. He asked for an interpreter to get more help to understand what’s going on.

Emilio’s from Venezuela originally, and they didn’t give an interpreter. It was only when the bus got to the Mexican border that he realized that, oh, I’m being dropped off in Mexico, a country where I am not from. He did not have a passport on him because he was detained at an asylum check-in.

There are definitely other instances as well. For example, people in ICE detention not having access to interpreters when they’re trying to get medical help just with regular interactions with guards. And there’s no public information on just how often deaf people are given interpreters.

However, there are definitely stories of people just not having access when they need it. Just imagine if you’re the only person who really speaks your language and you’re alone in ICE detention, and how much more brutal that is.

There’s another problem that would arise from sign language barriers, and that’s interpreters who can’t sign in the migrant’s language, right?

Yeah, and so this organization called Hands United, which helped deaf immigrants and their families, told me that the U.S. does not recognize certification for sign language interpreters for languages other than American Sign Language.

So interpreters are essentially taken at their word that they can actually interpret in another form of sign language, like Venezuelan Sign Language, Mexican Sign Language. This leads to people sometimes getting very poor-quality interpreters, because there’s just no certification process in the United States for that.

You know, something else that strikes me: There have been a lot of concern about the masking of ICE agents, especially when enforcement actions are taking place, and that unto itself, it would seem, would pose a barrier for many deaf migrants, no?

I spoke to the president of the National Hispanic Latino Association of the Deaf, and he told me about this being a major concern when you’re dealing with an ICE agent and they’re asking you questions.

By the way, it’s also not true that deaf people can read people’s lips perfectly. I feel like that’s a common misconception. But it is helpful, so when a deaf person doesn’t even have access to that, that just is a lot more scary because you don’t know what’s going on.

You also report that staff cuts have affected deaf migrants. Say more about that.

So there’s something called the Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, and when there’s a complaint that Section 504, that I previously mentioned, is not being followed, you’re supposed to be able to file a complaint there.

So there used to be around 150 staff members in this office under the Department of Homeland Security, and all but two were laid off last year, and so this office is basically not operating.

But this is happening at a time when ICE, as I understand it, has been staffing up.

Yeah absolutely and they basically completely just gutted the enforcement that’s supposed to look over whether or not people with disability accommodation, they’re being followed.

What comes next here, Julia? Are you seeing any momentum or movement on this issue?

I think there’s a problem faced when there’s a minority of people that face an issue.

It’s hard to necessarily get a large movement around something. There are not a lot of disability and deaf organizations that are doing work specifically focusing on helping deaf people in the immigration system. Hands United is a far minority of groups. So that’s definitely a challenge.

There’s not one clear way forward, but people are definitely trying. There are definitely lawsuits happening.

It’s a developing story, as they say.

I would say there’s not necessarily a clear end in sight to any of this, just because it’s definitely part of the deportation machine and there’s an not an end in sight for that either.
