On Saturday, the U.S. slapped 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of imports from Canada. In response, Carney announced tariffs on $20 billion of U.S. products beginning on September 8. Carney spoke to reporters on Saturday.

Reporter: “Why does it feel like today Mark Carney is going to war, trade war, the tone?”

Prime Minister Mark Carney: “Because we were attacked. Like, you’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked. The U.S. put 50%. We waited until the United States decided to actually implement these so-called 338 tariffs. That’s fine.”

We’ll have more on the U.S.-Canda trade war after headlines, when we’ll speak with Avi Lewis, the leader of the New Democratic Party in Canada, and Lori Wallach of the American Economic Liberties Project.

In Texas, calls are mounting to shut down the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, where it’s estimated more than 100 children are being detained by ICE. This comes after a 5-year-old boy, identified as Liam Tadeo, and his father were taken by ICE on their way to a child’s soccer game in Austin last week. Journalist Lidia Terrazas of Univision posted a video on social media showing Liam crying and his father handcuffed as they’re escorted into a vehicle. The arrest happened just days before Liam was set to start kindergarten. This is Texas Democratic Congressmember Greg Casar.

Rep. Greg Casar: ”ICE just arrested a 5-year-old boy on his way to a soccer game in my home city of Austin, Texas. His name, just like the name of the little boy from Minnesota, is Liam. And Liam should be starting kindergarten this week, but instead he’s sitting in a trailer prison right now in Dilley, Texas.”

Texas Democratic Congressmember Joaquin Castro said ICE denied his request to visit Liam and his father at the ICE camp. Castro said afterward, “His detention is another devastating example of why Dilley must be shut down and why our government must end the detention of children and families. I have seen firsthand the conditions that children and families are being subjected to at Dilley, and no child should be held there.” Dilley is run by the for-profit prison company CoreCivic.

More than 160 people have been deported to Haiti as the Trump administration begins to round up immigrants following the end of TPS, temporary protected status. It was the first deportation flight to Haiti after the Supreme Court greenlighted the Trump administration’s termination of TPS for an estimated 350,000 Haitians. The plane landed in the northern Haitian city of Cap-Haïtien Thursday. The country’s main international airport in Port-au-Prince has been deemed too dangerous due to gang violence and growing political instability. Many of those deported last week were TPS holders and had been living and working in the U.S. since 2010.

A U.S. Navy sailor who is on his ninth month of deployment aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln said his father has been detained by ICE. Joshua Aviles said he had received a call this weekend notifying him of his father’s arrest. Luis Manuel Aviles was taken into custody during a traffic stop in Key West, Florida. His wife said he is a handyman with a valid U.S. work permit. Aviles is originally from Nicaragua and has lived in the U.S. for nearly 20 years. His son Joshua said on social media, “This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only 'crime' was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”

Tyson Foods, the largest meatpacking and processing company in the U.S., has shuttered two of its facilities in Illinois and Utah, laying off more than 3,000 workers. The company said in a release earlier this month it’d be closing its Joslin, Illinois, and Eagle Mountain, Utah, facilities, claiming “one of the most historic cattle shortages the country has ever experienced” as the reason for the move. About 2,500 Tyson employees were impacted in Illinois alone due to the sudden closure of the plant. Workers and supporters held a rally in Joslin Friday in protest of the mass layoffs. They’re demanding the facility be reopened, as well as six months of full compensation and benefits for workers who’ve been left jobless. This comes as Tyson Foods CEO and President Donnie King made over $34 million in 2025, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In northwest Indiana, thousands of homes remain without power nearly two weeks after high winds and torrential rain knocked down trees and power lines, leaving behind flooded basements and roads. More than a third of a million homes and businesses were affected by the storm. This is Demond Pompy, a resident of hard-hit Gary, Indiana, where over one in three residents lived in poverty even before the disaster.

Desmond Pompy: “These are all the things that people take for granted, the basic things, as far as, like, power, taking a shower, flushing your toilet, anything of that nature like that. So, we’re really under siege, and I hope they just take care of the situation.”

A private arbitrator has ordered The Washington Post to rehire the opinion columnist Karen Attiah with back pay. Attiah was fired last fall over comments she made about the death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Her termination came as The Washington Post laid off more than 300 journalists, dismantling its sports, local news and international coverage — all under the ownership of billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. That followed Amazon’s $1 million donation to President Trump’s inaugural fund. Karen Attiah spoke to Democracy Now! in February.

Karen Attiah: “There’s a reason why this is an international news story. I think The Washington Post stands for a lot more than just a media company. It stands for a lot more than even just journalism, I would say. For a lot of people around the world, they’re looking at The Washington Post as a proxy and a bellwether for what’s happening to America and democracy.”

title: Trump administration moves to impose more than $100,000 fee for H-1B worker visas
description:

About 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February, according to court filings.
In imposing the fee, Trump invoked the president’s power under federal immigration law to restrict the entry of certain foreign nationals who would be detrimental to U.S. interests.

text:
Aug 24 (Reuters) – President Donald Trump’s administration on Monday released a proposed regulation to codify an unprecedented more than $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers that Trump first imposed last year but has been blocked by the courts.

The fee first imposed by Trump in a temporary proclamation last year vastly raises the cost of the visas that are heavily relied on in the tech, education and research sectors.

A federal judge in June ruled that the fee was illegal and blocked the Trump administration from collecting it. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision while a different court considers whether a judge in Washington, D.C., properly rejected a challenge to the fee by a major business group.

Trump’s 2025 proclamation imposing the fee expires in September, one year after it was issued, but directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to adopt regulations making it permanent.

The proposed $103,265 fee by DHS, posted online in the Federal Register on Monday to be formally published on Tuesday, kicks off a 30-day public comment period. The rule could be finalized by the end of the year.

The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty fields and offers 65,000 visas annually, with another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees, approved for three to six years.

The order Trump issued last year sharply increased the cost of obtaining some H-1B visas, which had typically come with about $2,000 to $5,000 in fees, depending on various factors.

DEBATE OVER VISA PROGRAM

Trump, a Republican, and other critics of the H-1B program say it is abused by many companies who replace American workers with cheaper foreign labor. But business groups and many individual companies have said the visa program is needed to address a lack of qualified American workers for some jobs and to allow U.S. businesses to recruit top talent.

About 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee on a total of 85 visa applications as of late February, according to court filings.

In imposing the fee, Trump invoked the president’s power under federal immigration law to restrict the entry of certain foreign nationals who would be detrimental to U.S. interests.

The fee is being challenged by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the largest U.S. business lobbying group, Democratic-led states and a coalition of unions and employers. Those lawsuits could be amended to challenge the rule proposed this week once it is finalized.

LEGAL CHALLENGES MOUNT

The lawsuits claim that Trump’s power to restrict entry does not allow him to override the law that created the H-1B visa program. The states and groups that sued also say that the Homeland Security Department cannot impose fees, taxes or other means to generate revenue for the United States without permission from Congress.

The Trump administration has maintained that the fee is not a traditional tax and that courts have little power to question the president’s authority to restrict entry into the country.

Amid Trump’s broader immigration crackdown, employers last year registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas, down more than 25% from 2024 and fewer than half of the 794,000 visas sought in 2023, according to data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The Trump administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed a new visa selection process that would favor higher-skilled and better-paid workers. Earlier in August, the Department of Homeland Security in a separate rule added fees of up to $4,500 to applications to extend the stay of H-1B workers or to transfer employees based in other countries to the United States.

(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, New York; Additional reporting by Daphne Psaledakis and Susan Heavey in Washington; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Matthew Lewis)

Dr. James J. Zogby ©

President

Arab American Institute

While the US has a long history of signing treaties, making commitments, and then walking away from them (ask Native American tribes about this), this century’s record of American policy in the Middle East is something quite extraordinary. Dramatic policy shifts, broken treaties, promises made and forgotten, foolish wars fought without attention paid to the mess left for others, and the shattering of international law and conventions—all of these have done substantial damage to the region and to the trust that others have in the US.

It’s convenient for Republicans and Democrats to point the finger at the “other side” for America’s loss of standing and support in the world. In reality, there’s plenty of blame to be shared by all of this century’s administrations. President George W. Bush started the disastrous wars and occupations of Afghanistan and Iraq, but Presidents Barack Obama and Joseph Biden ended both badly, compounding the damage that had been done. And while Bush may have flaunted international law and conventions with the use of torture, rendition, and extrajudicial targeted killings, Obama further undermined the US’s commitment to the rule of law by refusing to call for accountability for these crimes.

Biden waxed eloquent in his defense of what he called the “international rules-based order.” But he undercut himself when it became clear that his commitment was selective since it only applied to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and not to Israel’s genocidal policies in Palestine.

And speaking of Palestine, during the first quarter of this century, no administration has taken the firm measures needed to curb Israeli behaviors in the occupied Palestinian territories or in Lebanon and now Syria. The impact has been clear: Israel acts with impunity, Palestinians have lost hope, and the people of the region have lost even a shred of belief that the US can play a constructive role in peacemaking.

Upon this dismal record of this century’s first four administrations, President Donald Trump, since reentering the White House in 2025, has pounded the final nail in the coffin of trust for American leadership in the Middle East.

While on one occasion Biden went to UN Security Council and secured passage of a ceasefire for Gaza—telling the council that Israel approved it, knowing full well that Israel had not agreed to its terms—Trump has taken this practice of dissembling even further. With great fanfare he assembled leaders to an event celebrating his 20-point peace plan to end the Gaza conflict. The problem, of course, was that none of the combatant parties—neither Hamas nor especially Israel—had agreed to its terms. And Trump’s boastful handling of his war with Iran has reached new levels of absurdity. On at least 42 occasions he has announced that the war was over, he had won, or that Iran was begging to negotiate on his terms, only to pivot a day or two later threatening, in violent or vulgar language, to obliterate Iran if they didn’t, as he put it, “wave the white flag” of surrender.

Added to this mess are the thousands of Lebanese who’ve been killed and the scores of villages laid waste by Israel since the Trump-backed ceasefire, the displacement and frightening violence that Israeli settlers and soldiers are wreaking in the West Bank, the continuing genocide unfolding in Gaza, and the insecurity in the Arab Gulf States housing US bases which are being recklessly attacked by Iranian missiles and drones. It is no wonder that Arabs have lost faith not only in the US’s commitment to regional peace and security, but also to the trustworthiness of the US as an ally.

A problem so big can’t be fixed by one US election. After decades of a dizzying roller coaster ride of wars based on lies, violations of international laws and conventions, promises made and then broken, and now an administration that acts impulsively and makes contradictory pronouncements as if words have no meaning—trust has been lost.

After the disasters resulting from the Bush administration’s Iraq war, its anti-Arab, anti-Muslim domestic policies, and its ill-conceived “democracy agenda,” President Obama traveled to Cairo to deliver a speech designed to open a new chapter in US relations with the region. After seven years without decisive follow-through on the promises he’d made in his Cairo address, Obama gave a long interview to The Atlantic Magazine in which he blamed the Arabs for not doing enough. When I spoke with him about the speech and that interview, he told me that the expectations of the Arabs had been too high. I responded that he was the one who set the high expectations and made the promises that he would “change Washington, change America, and change the world.” “Don’t blame them,” I said, “for believing you.”

What’s evident now is that the Arab world isn’t believing US promises or even our words. They are beginning to find their way in a post-US world order by creating new alliances, finding new partners, and putting their own interests first. If the US is to even have a place in this new order, we will need more than a just a new president with promises of change. What will be required is a thoughtful examination of our decades of shortcomings and betrayals leading to new policies toward justice for Palestinians and regional partnerships and security. But acknowledging the problems is only the first step. A demonstrated and sustained commitment to implement a changed approach to the multiple crises we have helped to create or exacerbate across the region must follow. Since it took us a generation to dig deep holes for ourselves in the Arab World, getting out won’t be quick or easy. Restoring trust will take time and hard work.

text:
BILLINGS — The chants were hard to miss Sunday evening in downtown Billings.

“ICE out!”

A small group with the Billings Alliance for Immigrant Rights gathered on a downtown street corner, calling for an end to federal immigration enforcement in Billings and demanding local leaders establish a sanctuary city.

The group, which has been pressing the Billings City Council on the issue for months, said recent immigration arrests in the community have made its push more urgent.

“We felt it was urgent to hold an emergency rally to demand ICE out of Billings and demand Sanctuary City now,” said Lain Dorsey, who is with the Billings Alliance for Immigrant Rights.

The rally comes days after a father and his young daughter were detained by federal immigration agents outside a United Way of Yellowstone County back-to-school distribution event.

United Way officials have said they did not know the two had been detained until the following day and are now reevaluating security for future events.

For Dorsey and other immigration rights advocates, the incident underscores their concerns about the growing presence of federal immigration agents in Billings.

“We won't accept this in Billings,” Dorsey said. “But as long as this continues, we'll be out here demanding a Sanctuary City and putting pressure on our local officials to make that happen.”

Dorsey said the group has repeatedly asked the city council to meet with them, but has not received a meeting.

The protesters were met with a mixed reaction from passing drivers Sunday. Some honked in support while others expressed disapproval.

Dorsey said the support is encouraging, but the group's larger goal is to build enough public pressure to push city leaders to act.

“What we're really fighting for is to build a real movement that can put pressure on city council to install a sanctuary city so that everybody can be safe,” Dorsey said.

The group says it is fighting for what it calls “legalization for all” and wants immigrants in Billings to be able to live without fear of deportation.

The rally comes amid a broader debate over the role of federal immigration enforcement in Montana.

Republican U.S. Sen. Steve Daines has defended federal immigration enforcement, saying in a recent Fox News interview that the country is safer because of federal law enforcement.

Meanwhile, Paul Pope, a political science professor at Montana State University Billings, told MTN News last week that the rapid expansion of immigration enforcement has raised questions about training and due process.

“We've seen people deported who have not actually violated any laws,” Pope said.

He also raised concerns that law enforcement training has been curtailed as federal agencies work to put more agents on the streets.

Dorsey said the Billings Alliance for Immigrant Rights plans to continue organizing until the city establishes a sanctuary city.

“We'll continue to be out here until immigrants in our community do not have to fear that they'll be deported by ICE or Border Patrol and that they can actually live a life of dignity where they don't have to live in fear,” Dorsey said.

Two Ecuadorian women who were injured in a rollover crash in Central Florida were taken into immigration custody after being discharged from a hospital, with family members saying they were questioned about their legal status while receiving treatment.

Grace Stephanie Calero Cabanilla, 39, and her daughter, Giulianna Mía Carriel Calero, 19, were involved in a crash on August 20 at Marigold Avenue and Sheldrake Road in Poinciana, according to affidavits obtained from the Polk County Sheriff's Office.

Calero Cabanilla's cousin, Jonathan Bravo, 37, told Newsweek that she was driving to work with her daughter when another vehicle struck the passenger side of their car in a crash that he said they "almost died" in.

Read More on News

"It was a very severe accident," Bravo said. "The car was completely totaled."

Bravo said the impact caused the vehicle to roll about four times. He said its wheels and trunk came off and its front end was severely damaged.

A spokesperson for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) told Newsweek that Calero Cabanilla entered the United States legally on March 8, 2023, but overstayed her authorized period of admission. The agency said Carriel Calero entered legally on February 8, 2025, but overstayed her period of admission.

The women were transported by ambulance to HCA Florida Poinciana Hospital after the crash.

Bravo said Calero Cabanilla and her daughter were placed in separate rooms after arriving at the hospital. He said that a Polk County sheriff’s deputy began questioning Calero Cabanilla about her immigration status shortly after she arrived, while she was wearing a neck brace and had been given medication.

"She was in bed with a neck brace, trying to receive the proper medical attention that she needs," Bravo said.

HCA Florida Poinciana Hospital told Newsweek in a statement its "focus and priority always is taking care of every patient that comes through our emergency room doors regardless of immigration status" and that its employees are dedicated to providing "compassionate care to every patient."

"Like all hospitals, we are required to comply with laws and regulations that govern interactions with verified members of law enforcement when they enter our hospital," a spokesperson said. "At all times and no matter the situation, we do not deviate from our goal of providing the medical care our patients need and deserve."

"As part of a crash investigation on Thursday, deputies went to the local hospital to speak with the occupants of one of the vehicles," a spokesperson for the Polk County Sheriff's Office told Newsweek. "As the deputies were obtaining information from those involved, it was discovered that the driver is in the United States illegally from Ecuador after overstaying an expired visa by several years."

The sheriff's office said deputies subsequently determined that the driver's adult daughter, who was also involved in the crash, had overstayed a visa.

"ICE issued detainers for both women, and after the women were discharged from the hospital, they were taken into custody and transported to the Polk County Jail," the spokesperson added.

ICE separately confirmed to Newsweek that detainers were lodged against both women following the crash.

"ICE lodged detainers for Grace Stephanie Calero Cabanilla and Giulianna Mía Carriel Calero, illegal aliens from Ecuador, after they were arrested by the Polk County Sheriff’s Office following a traffic accident," an agency spokesperson said.

Bravo said Calero Cabanilla has a pending asylum application and work authorization and that Carriel Calero was included in her mother's asylum case.

"My cousin was legally working," Bravo said. "She applied for asylum; they provided her with a work permit, with a Social Security number."

Bravo also said Carriel Calero's visa document was valid through 2030.

Arrest affidavits reviewed by Newsweek say that deputies responding to the crash identified immigration holds for both women and contacted ICE Officer Joel Jean, who confirmed civil immigration warrants. The documents say that both women had no criminal history and were taken into custody and transported to the Polk County Sheriff's Office Processing Center.

A spokesperson for the Polk County Sheriff's Office said the agency could not provide the crash report because Florida law exempts such reports from public release for the first 60 days following a crash. When asked whether the other driver involved in the crash had been cited, arrested or charged, the Sheriff's Office declined to comment.

The case comes as the Trump administration has expanded immigration enforcement and sought to increase cooperation between federal authorities and state and local law enforcement agencies under its mass deportation policy. Through programs such as Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, certain state and local officers, after receiving federal training and authorization, can perform specified immigration enforcement functions under ICE supervision, including identifying people who may be subject to removal proceedings and coordinating their transfer into federal custody. The administration has also expanded immigration enforcement beyond traditional criminal-enforcement priorities, with visa overstays and other immigration-status violations increasingly subject to federal scrutiny and enforcement.

Calero Cabanilla's affidavit states that a Law Enforcement Support Center verification found she was "not legally in the USA, subject to removal, has an open case for removal proceedings." Both affidavits conclude that "upon the conclusion of my investigation, no further action was taken."

Neither affidavit alleges that either woman committed a crime related to the crash.

Bravo said Calero Cabanilla suffered injuries to her neck, back, arm, legs and knees and was still in pain when officers took her into custody.

"As they took out my cousin, she was screaming that her arm was hurting," he said.

Bravo also alleged that Carriel Calero suffered multiple seizures at the hospital and had initially been expected to remain there for further treatment.

He further alleged that officers removed Carriel Calero from the hospital early the following morning while she was still wearing a hospital gown and that family members recorded portions of the encounter.

Video of the incident shows law enforcement officers physically separating and detaining the two women inside the hospital room. At the start of the clip, Carriel Calero sits on a gurney wearing a blue hospital gown, clinging tightly around the waist of her mother, who is dressed in a light blue button-down shirt and jeans. Multiple officers surround the bed and forcibly pull the women apart as Carriel Calero, screams in distress.

Two officers hold Carriel Calero, down on the gurney while another officer pulls her mother off the bed, holding her by the arms. As she is pulled away, she cries out and asks to see documentation. The camera then follows into the hallway, recording her as she is escorted down the corridor by officers with her hands secured behind her back.

In another video recorded by family members, relatives confront a Polk County Sheriff's deputy in the hospital hallway as Calero Cabanilla, is led away in handcuffs. The person recording and other family members demand to see an arrest warrant or legal documentation authorizing the detainment, asking repeatedly, "Where's the paper?" and "Where's the arrest warrant, sir?"

The deputy responds that they "don't have to show it to you, sir." The family member recording challenges the deputy further, stating that Calero Cabanilla "almost died in that accident," accusing the initial officer of questioning her while she was in shock without identifying himself as working with ICE, and noting that Carriel Calero suffers from anxiety attacks.

Bravo said the women were initially held in Polk County and that they had later been transferred to Pinellas County.

He also said relatives attempted to provide Carriel Calero with prescribed psychiatric medication while she was in custody but were told it would not be accepted. It was not immediately clear whether she subsequently received the medication or other medical treatment.

Bravo said Calero Cabanilla worked in marketing and that Carriel Calero had planned to complete credits required for her high school diploma before the crash.

He said Calero Cabanilla is divorced, Carriel Calero is her only child, and both women are from Guayaquil.

The family is raising money for legal representation and medical expenses on GoFundMe. Bravo said they had not yet retained an attorney and that neither woman currently had an immigration hearing scheduled, though Calero Cabanilla had been awaiting a hearing in her asylum case.

"We just want the truth to be out there," Bravo said. "We want justice for them."

"As a family, we're distraught, we feel so unsafe in this country now. We feel so unsafe that even in the hospitals, you know, where you're supposed to feel safe."

ICE said both women would remain in custody pending removal proceedings.

text:
Plans to supply Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers with special gloves that can deliver electric shocks have alarmed experts and drawn scrutiny amid some high-profile lawsuits over their use in local correctional facilities.

In one extreme case, a 43-year-old man died after allegedly being shocked 40 times by officers with a combination of the gloves and a Taser in a county jail in Kentucky, and the man’s widow is suing authorities.

Earlier this month, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, published plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to outfit ICE officers by March of next year with the controversial gloves, which are also used in various police departments and some schools.

Civil rights advocates protest that the federal agency’s use of force during Donald Trump’s immigration crackdowns already lacks proper oversight.

ICE “is putting these [gloves] in the hands of an agency that has dropped its hiring standards, its training, its background requirements in its hiring spree”, Sarah Mehta, deputy director of government affairs in the equality division of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), said.

“We’re already seeing the consequences of that in lawless and violent enforcement actions in our streets,” she told the Guardian.

“What’s really terrifying is use of them on the streets, potentially to terrify people, to create a chilling effect. But what’s also scary is what [their] uses will be where we can’t see them. We don’t know how they’re going to be used in places like Fort Bliss,”she added, referring to the largest migrant detention facility in the US, where allegations of abuse are legion. The government denies claims of any inhumane conditions.

Mehta further said of the gloves: “There are no circumstances where we think their use is appropriate.”

The device carries the brand name G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and is manufactured by Compliant Technologies, a company owned by military veterans and based in Lexington, Kentucky. The glove is known as a conductive distraction and de-escalation deviceand can only be sold to certain verified entities, such as law enforcement, corrections, security, military, and emergency medical services (EMS) personnel, and requires training. It works by delivering an electric shock when the user pushes a button on the glove and touches or grips bare skin.

In one demonstration video, a man gives a brief, light touch for approximately one second to the lower back of a prone volunteer, who jerks his body and cries out: “Ow, fuck”.

Compliant Technologies has posted multiple video demonstrations on its Instagram page. In one video from November 2025, a woman wearing the glove grips firmly on the exposed forearm of a volunteer man for about two seconds. The man buckles to the ground, shouting expletives and says “Let me go!”

“I’m going to comply any time,” the man says from the ground in a half-humorous tone to the team running the demonstration. Jeff Niklaus, founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, can be seen laughing in the video as the man fell to the ground. “Say that louder,” he says.

The man, seemingly a prospective customer, says: “Yeah, we need that [product].”

Compliant Technologies did not respond to a series of questions and requests for comment from the Guardian.

A DHS spokesperson sent this statement in response to questions: “ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country.

“Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards.”

The minimum voltage for the CT-G5 model is 324 volts, and the maximum is 380 volts. A Taser, by contrast, can typically fire prongs from a distance to incapacitate someone with 1,200 to 1,500 volts.

The glove user manual instructs wearers to avoid using the product on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and disabled people.

The gloves have been deployed to a limited extent in law enforcement, healthcare, and even some educational environments across the country. An estimated 50 police departments across 20 states are using the technology, according to an NPR analysis.

In May 2025, the Omaha police department purchased 40 pairs of gloves to be used in public schools for just under $66,000, according to city documents. The department confirmed in a statement that 29 of its 34 school resource officers (SROs) – typically police providing security full time in schools – have trained in use of the gloves and work in public middle and high schools.

A representative from the Omaha police department shared with the Guardian the report from an incident where the G.L.O.V.E. was used. The report says a female SRO used the shock glove on a male middle school student based on his “highly aggressive and assaultive behavior”. The officer placed the glove on the student’s forearm twice, once for one second, and then again for two to three seconds, which, the report continued, caused the student to drop to the floor, face down.

According to the report, the SRO asked if the student needed medical assistance after being shocked, and he said no.

Last week, Omaha police acceded to a request from the school superintendent to discontinue the gloves in Omaha, Nebraska’s largest public school district, NBC reported.

In a very different example, Joshua Elswick, formerly detained at the Bullitt county jail in Shepherdsville, near Louisville, Kentucky, sued Lt Ryan Derrough alleging excessive force, after Derrough, a guard, used the gloves on Elswick during pre-trial detention.

Elswick, who has paranoid schizophrenia and other serious mental illnesses, according to the lawsuit, was arrested and booked into jail in September 2022 after a domestic dispute involving methamphetamine use. Derrough and another deputy attempted to remove Elswick’s handcuffs and leg shackles before formally taking him into custody, but Elswick was paranoid that the officers were going to kill him and he resisted, whereupon Derrough shocked Elswick with the gloves, according to the lawsuit. The incident can be seen in surveillance footage featured in a report on the case from Kentucky TV station WDRB.

The footage shows a tense scene, with the guard wearing bright yellow gloves and using them on Elswick, who is struggling against three guards, and yells out.

The Kentucky federal court dismissed Elswick’s lawsuit in June 2025, finding that Derrough’s use of force was warranted, a decision upheld by an appeals court in January.

A representative for APB Consulting Solutions, a dealer and training partner for Compliant Technologies’ product, told WDRB in 2022 that agencies undergo a lot of training and that used properly the gloves can prevent further injury – while it is recommended not to apply them for more than 15 seconds.

Sara Collins, a lawyer representing Elswick, declined to comment on the specific civil case, but told the Guardian: “With proper training and use, effective, less-lethal force options are much-needed resources in law enforcement. Shock gloves, however, are not a new tool.”

“I am troubled by the fact that the overwhelming majority of law enforcement agencies across the country do not use them,” she added, noting that relatively few departments out of 18,000 across the US have bought the gloves.

“Feasibility, practicality, training, risk of error, and intent are among my many concerns about their implementation by ICE,” Collins said.

Meanwhile, Johnathan Mansfield, who was arrested on a public intoxication charge in 2024, suffered a cardiac arrest two weeks after he was allegedly shocked 27 times with the gloves and 13 times by a Taser at Madison county detention center in Richmond, Kentucky, according to the lawsuit filed by Mansfield’s family against the authorities, claiming wrongful death.

The complaint alleges: “An internal investigation by the Madison County Detention Center found that ‘ ... Mr Manfield [sic] suffered a cardiac arrest following the series of Taser and G.L.O.V.E. exposures.’”

The internal investigation, as cited in the lawsuit, stated that “four distinct use of force incidents were recorded… resulting in a total of 13 taser exposures – comprising both probes and drive-stun applications – lasting between 23 to 28 seconds. Additionally, there were 27 exposures using the G.L.O.V.E.”

One of the shock glove exposures lasted for 45 seconds and another for 99 seconds, the document alleges.

The suit, filed in a Madison county, Kentucky circuit court, is still pending.
