text:
A federal judge in New York has vacated a Trump administration policy that suspended the processing of visas from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, whose nationals the Trump administration deemed likely to require public assistance in the United States.

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, set aside the policy Friday as “contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority by issuing the policy, which “runs afoul” of the Immigration and Nationality Act by mandating “the refusal of visas to eligible applicants without any basis in law,” the judge ruled.

Judge says power lies with consular officers

Vargas said the policy also undermines the congressional requirement that puts consular officers at the forefront of any visa decision.

“Congress imbued these officers with exclusive authority and discretion to determine if an immigrant is eligible for a visa based upon review of specific and detailed criteria set forth in the statute,” she wrote. “The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme.”

The policy was challenged by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals, including six whose family members had been refused visas. The remaining five are outside the country and had filed “employment-based petitions” to come to the United States.

Advocates say keeping families apart is cruel

“We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together,” said Anna Gallagher, the executive director of CLINIC, a national nonprofit that provides training, resources, and support to a network of immigration legal service providers and was one of the plaintiffs.

“Catholic social teaching calls us to uphold the dignity of every person and recognize the family as the foundation of society,” she said in a statement. “This decision affirms both those values and the rule of law, allowing families to once again move forward toward reunification.”

Another plaintiff is African Communities Together, a Harlem-based nonprofit. One of its leaders called the ruling “a tremendous victory for the rule of law.”

“This unlawful and racist ban caused immeasurable harm, cruelly keeping families and loved ones apart,” Diana Konate, deputy executive director for policy and advocacy, said in a statement. “Today, we are elated to tell our community members: this ban is no more.”

Trump expands his anti-immigration agenda

President Donald Trump has imposed a growing list of immigration and travel bans mostly for people from Africa, Asia and Latin America. The State Department said Saturday that the Trump administration is “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants,” and that it would not comment on pending litigation.

At the time the policy was issued, the State Department said it had instructed consular officers to halt immigrant visa applications from the 75 countries in accordance with a broader order in November that tightened rules around potential immigrants who might become “public charges.” Relying on Council of Economic Advisers data, the State Department said that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from these countries received some form of public assistance.

A separate notice sent to all U.S. embassies and consulates said that non-immigrant visa applicants also should be “fully vetted and screened” for the possibility that they might seek public benefits in the United States.

The cable, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, noted several times that the applicant must prove they won’t apply for public benefits while in the U.S., and that consular officers who suspect the applicant might apply should require them to fill out a form proving their financial bona fides.

title: Judge bars effort to 'conscript' locals into ICE cooperation - Law & Crime
description:
A federal judge on Friday dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against a Michigan county that adamantly refused to cooperate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The lawsuit alleged the county had "become a sanctuary from the enforcement of federal immigration law and a harbor to removable criminal aliens."
The judge notes the INA "contemplates the possibility of state and local cooperation with federal immigration officials, but it generally does not require cooperation with any particular federal request."
But the Trump administration insisted several Washtenaw policies enacted between 2021 and 2026 amounted to "obstruction of lawful federal immigration operations" and argued "local laws must yield."
The defendants expressly do not honor detainer requests unless they are accompanied with a valid judicial warrant signed by a judge.
text:
A federal judge on Friday dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against a Michigan county that adamantly refused to cooperate with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

On April 9, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a 53-page complaint against Washtenaw County, along with various officials and agencies, including the local sheriff's office. The lawsuit alleged the county had "become a sanctuary from the enforcement of federal immigration law and a harbor to removable criminal aliens."

"The challenged policies and actions…are invalid under the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution and therefore must not be permitted to further obstruct the efforts of federal immigration law enforcement to carry out its mission assigned by Congress," the original petition reads.

Now, U.S. District Judge F. Kay Behm, a Joe Biden appointee, has tossed the lawsuit for failure to state a claim in an 86-page opinion and order that grants the defendants' motion to dismiss in full.

"The Constitution imparts much authority on the federal government," the judge mused. "But neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will."

The court, in a lengthy analysis, views a great deal of the issues through the lens of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

The judge notes the INA "contemplates the possibility of state and local cooperation with federal immigration officials, but it generally does not require cooperation with any particular federal request."

To that end, the court continues, localities that "disagree with the President's mass deportation scheme and have ended prior cooperation agreements with the federal government" have, as of late, largely left "federal immigration enforcement to federal officers and agencies – and have enacted policies to that end."

But the Trump administration insisted several Washtenaw policies enacted between 2021 and 2026 amounted to "obstruction of lawful federal immigration operations" and argued "local laws must yield."

The judge offered an uncharitable summary of ICE's perspective.

"Unwilling to take 'no' for an answer, the federal government now insists that the INA does not offer localities a choice at all," the opinion goes on. "Apparently flummoxed by the County's decision to focus its resources on local priorities and public safety, the United States sues to demand Washtenaw County's cooperation, the use of its jail cells, and its resources."

In one major point of dispute, the DOJ argued the defendants should be forced to comply with detainers issued by ICE agents.

The defendants expressly do not honor detainer requests unless they are accompanied with a valid judicial warrant signed by a judge.

"Forcing Defendants to honor detainer requests would require the County to use its limited 'law enforcement time, resources, and custodial facilities to arrest and hold individuals purely for federal civil immigration purposes,' — possibly in violation of the Fourth Amendment," the defendants argued.

The court, for its part, declined to rule on the Fourth Amendment issue because the detainer dispute was solved otherwise.

First Behm consults the anti-commandeering doctrine:

The government's preferred reading of the INA envisions that all local enforcement nationwide must track their detainees' immigration status (and any information that might conceivably have a future impact on that status), and then use their jail cells to hold those detainees pursuant to detainers authorized by the INA. But if local law enforcement were to in any way fail in their alleged duties to enforce federal law and promote the President's mass deportation scheme, the President lacks any authority to remove those persons, hire replacements, or control their actions in any meaningful sense…the government offers no way out.

In a dovetailing preemption analysis, the court also found that another disputed policy "does not purport to 'prohibit' or 'restrict' any state or local official from sending, maintaining, or exchanging information regarding the immigration status of any individual."

The court also found the local laws do not run afoul of the intergovernmental immunity doctrine — which bars state or local rules that regulate the federal government or discriminate against it.

"[T]hat ICE may use detainers consistent with the INA does not compel the conclusion that state or local officials must comply with those requests," the court goes on. "If the statute does not mandate compliance with the detainer, then the mere choice of a locality not to cooperate with detainer requests does not 'regulate' the federal government in any meaningful sense."

Since the court ruled on a motion to dismiss and in the defendants' favor in full, the opinion closes the case at the district court level.

text:
A Cameroonian man who was twice rejected for refugee status and faced deportation under Japan’s tighter immigration rules will be allowed to stay in the country after winning his lawsuit against the government.

His case was one of at least six in which courts overturned government decisions to deny refugee status for foreign applicants in 2025, support groups said.

They said the court decisions raise questions about the revised system under which those who have applied for refugee status for a third time could be deported.

In the Cameroonian’s case, the Tokyo District Court in June last year rejected the government’s assessment that turned down his refugee status applications and ordered the state to recognize him as a refugee.

The Tokyo High Court upheld the ruling in April, and it was finalized in May.

The man said he was both happy and disappointed at the same time because the process had taken such a long time.

The ruling said the man, who lived in a minority, English-speaking region of Cameroon, was arrested and detained by police four times because he was active in an anti-government group. He was tortured on three of the occasions.

He came to Japan in 2012 and twice applied for refugee status but was rejected both times.

The government said his accounts lacked credibility and argued against his refugee status.

Both the district and high courts, however, found his accounts credible and concluded he qualifies as a refugee because he could be persecuted upon repatriation.

Lawyer Chie Komai, who represented the Cameroonian, said the man’s arguments and central evidence have remained the same since he first applied for refugee status.

Komai said the government and the judiciary gave opposite decisions because they assessed those materials differently.

“Similar discrepancies in assessments could throw applicants’ lives out of kilter,” she argued.

The man applied for refugee status for a third time in April 2023, about half a year before he went to court.

An amended Immigration Control and Refugee Recognition Law took effect in June 2024, just as his case was being tried in the district court.

Under the new system, applicants denied on their third or subsequent attempt to gain refugee status would be deported, in principle.

Japan had previously suspended deportations for all applicants. The government said one reason it changed the system was that unqualified people were repeatedly applying just to stay in Japan.

“The man could have been deported if he had failed to win the case,” Komai said. “The current system could end up deporting those who should qualify for refugee protection.”

The United Nations sent a letter to the Japanese government in 2023, arguing that this system, which had yet to take effect, “would fall short of international human rights standards.”

The government replied that the system has no problems because “foreign nationals applying for refugee status for three or more times ... have been denied applications twice or more after full examinations ..., which means that it is not necessary to stabilize their legal status.”

Officials with the Japan Lawyers Network for Refugees said courts of first instance, intermediate appeal and final appeal delivered 46 decisions in 2024 in lawsuits over government denials of refugee status.

The plaintiffs won at least seven of those cases, including two in which they had applied for refugee status at least three times, the officials said.

“Some have been denied refugee recognition and have yet to go to court,” said Shogo Watanabe, a lawyer who heads JLNR. “I believe there are even more people who qualify as refugees but have not been recognized as such by the government.”

Japan’s refugee recognition rate is extremely low compared to corresponding figures for other nations in the advanced world.

Refugee status was recognized for only 183 of the 9,397 applicants who received screening results in 2025.

“Toughening deportations, even though nobody knows if the refugee applications are being screened properly, could jeopardize the lives of applicants,” Watanabe said. “The current system should be reviewed.”

Liam Tadeo and his dad are in the country illegally.

The five-year-old boy, identified by his family as Liam Tadeo, appears to be crying as he tried to hold the hand of his handcuffed father being escorted to an unmarked vehicle. The boy and his father are now being held at the Dilley Detention Center in Texas.

CNN affiliate Univision spoke with the mother of Liam, who chose not to be identified, and filmed a phone call she had with her detained-son.

“I love you so much and I miss you so much, my love,” the mother told Liam in Spanish. “Don’t despair, my love, okay?”

“Okay,” the boy said.

“I love you so, so much, my love,” the mother said.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Nieto had previously self-deported after he was arrested in 2025 and he then made his way back into the country. They also insisted children held at Dilley have access to teachers, classrooms, and books.

“Martinez Nieto and his son will remain together in ICE custody pending removal. text:
Tampa, FL – On August 20, community members spoke at a Tampa City Council meeting demanding they pass an ordinance to end ICE cooperation.

The Tampa Police Department and ICE cooperate based on a federal 287(g) agreement. A 287(g) agreement creates a formal partnership that allows ICE to deputize local law enforcement to carry out the duties of federal immigration enforcement officers.

“I have been speaking with my neighbors, with church leaders, business owners and everyday Tampa residents. There’s always one thing that keeps coming up in the conversations and it is the impact of ICE in our city and in our neighborhoods,” Erain Boxtha, a member of Tampa Immigrants Rights Committee (IRC) stated.

Boxtha continued, “We are seeing businesses lose traffic because of ICE activity in our community. Churches closing because of impacted communities. And we are seeing families torn apart and left to pick up the pieces.”

Tampa City Councilmember Bill Carlson commented on the public’s opposition to the 287(g) agreement, saying, “it was not an act of city council” and “city council is very limited in what we can do.”

The 287(g)-agreement was signed in the spring of 2025 between TPD and ICE under Tampa Mayor Jane Castor and the Tampa Police Chief Lee Bercaw. They have the power to cancel the agreement.

Tampa IRC continues the fight to end local police cooperation with ICE. They are educating the public and targeting the city council, Tampa Mayor Jane Castor, and the new police chief.

Members of the Tampa Immigrants Rights Committee, along with individuals from Indivisible Pinellas, League of Women Voters and Partido Nacionalista de Puerto Rico, all spoke on public record.

text:
This article was republished with permission from WTOP’s news partners at Maryland Matters. Read the story at Maryland Matters.

WASHINGTON — Fentanyl seizures decreased by 39% during the first year of the second Trump administration after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shifted the Department of Homeland Security’s criminal investigations arm to conducting immigration enforcement, according to a report government investigators published Friday.

Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, a subagency of DHS’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement, reported an “all hands-on deck” environment toward immigration enforcement began in January 2025, according to the DHS Office of Inspector General report.

“With ICE dedicating more staff hours to immigration investigations, staffing hours for fentanyl investigations declined,” the report said.

The report found that the hours dedicated to fentanyl investigations for fiscal 2025 declined by more than 250,000 hours, or 31%, compared to fiscal 2024.

“At the same time, immigration enforcement saw the largest increase across all investigative categories, rising more than 1.7 million hours (over 800%),” according to the report.

Inspectors interviewed more than 100 agents from 11 HSI field offices for the report.

At one HSI office, approximately 99% of work was dedicated to immigration, leaving almost no capacity for fentanyl investigations, the watchdog found. A drug investigation team of seven agents was reduced to about three and the rest of the personnel was reassigned to work on immigration cases, according to the report.

Fentanyl is a highly addictive synthetic opioid that is the main driver of overdose deaths in the United States. HSI plays a key role in countering fentanyl smuggling in the U.S. by targeting routes, laboratories and collaborating with law enforcement to investigate smuggling operations.

ICE agrees

The inspector general recommended that HSI review staffing levels “to ensure an appropriate level of coverage commensurate with the relative priority of fentanyl investigations.”

Inspector general reports are presented to the affected agency for comment ahead of publication. ICE agreed with the recommendations in the DHS OIG report.

“Homeland Security Investigations will review staffing levels, and determine and implement next steps, as needed, to ensure an appropriate level of coverage commensurate with the relative priority of fentanyl investigations,” ICE’s comments in the report read.

ICE estimated that recommendation would be completed by June 2027.

The report also found that the technology HSI agents and analysts used had limitations during fentanyl investigations and their missions were “hindered by delays in agents obtaining funds to purchase information and evidence (i.e., drugs) during an investigation; a lack of independent authority to investigate fentanyl-related offenses; and low, inconsistent referral of fentanyl cases from U.S. Customs and Border Protection to HSI.”

text:
Trump border czar Tom Homan denied accusations that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents racially profile the people they target.

Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany played a clip on Saturday’s episode of Saturday in America of Democratic Socialists of America candidate Angie Nixon (D-FL), who’s running in the special election for U.S. Senate, discussing ICE and profiling.

Nixon told the Miami Community Newspapers Podcast, “We’re Black, [ICE is] gonna profile us, too.”

She continued, “They can’t tell the difference between an African-American or, you know, a Black American that is a descendant of slaves here in this country, or someone from Jamaica or Nigeria. Like, they are going to racially profile us, and they are going to escalate things, and they are going to shoot and kill us.”

McEnany asked Homan what he thought of Nixon’s assertion.

“That’s a ridiculous statement,” Homan said. “Look, we don’t racially profile. Everybody we talk to we have reasonable suspicion of aliens to talk to them. And to arrest them, we need probable cause. That’s what the law says and that’s we do. We don’t arrest people based on the color of their skin.”

Homan said he’s an “equal opportunity deporter.”

“I’m actually an equal opportunity deporter,” he said. “I deported people to 180 countries last year. So, I don’t care if you’re from Asia, you’re from Europe, or you’re from other countries. If you’re in the country illegally, you’ll be deported, regardless of the color of your skin.”

Homan then lamented about how hard so-called sanctuary cities make it for ICE agents to operate.

“This is why, Kayleigh, we’ve got so many ICE agents out there. This is why we flooded the zone of sanctuary cities. Because if they don’t let us take apprehension of the bad guy in the safety and security of the jail, right? So, they’re going to release him, now I’ve got to send a whole team of six or seven people to go look for this person in the community,” he said.

Homan continued:

So, what sanctuary cities do is not only protect, give sanctuary to criminals, it makes the community less safe because they’re releasing public safety threats back into the public, and they don’t have to. It puts our officers at greater risk. It puts the alien at greater risk. Cause anything can happen during a street arrest. So, this is why we’re flooding the zone, this is why we’re concentrating most of our resources in sanctuary cities, because we have to go into the community to find people we should have gotten in jail.

Watch above via Fox News.

title: The long and winding road to US citizenship and why legal status no longer cuts it
description:
Temporary Protected Status has allowed immigrants from countries facing war, natural disasters and other dangerous conditions to live and work legally in the United States.
Four categories of nonimmigrant status Meyer generally divides noncitizens into four broad categories.
TPS provides temporary protection from deportation and allows eligible recipients to work legally in the United States.
Applicants also must establish that they are not legally inadmissible to the United States.
A person may have lived and worked legally in the United States for years while remaining only temporarily protected from deportation.
text:
Temporary Protected Status has allowed immigrants from countries facing war, natural disasters and other dangerous conditions to live and work legally in the United States. But a recent Supreme Court ruling shows TPS can be given and taken away.

The Supreme Court recently handed down a ruling allowing the administration to revoke humanitarian protections for Somalian, Haitian, Ethiopian and Syrian nationals, as well as several other African nations.

The cases lay bare a fundamental clash in the U.S. immigration system: being legally allowed to live and work in the United States is not necessarily the same as having a path to permanent residency or citizenship.

Katie Meyer, director of the Immigration Law Clinic at Washington University in St. Louis and a professor of practice, said understanding the citizenship process requires first understanding the different immigration statuses people can hold.

“Before we can talk about citizenship, we really need to talk about the various types of statuses a non-citizen who’s in the U.S. might hold,” Meyer said.

Four categories of nonimmigrant status

Meyer generally divides noncitizens into four broad categories.

The first is nonimmigrant visa holders, including tourists, students, medical workers and temporary or seasonal employees. Most of those visas are not designed to lead to permanent residency or citizenship.

The second category includes immigrants seeking lawful permanent residence, commonly known as green card holders. They generally qualify through family relationships, employment or the diversity visa lottery.

The third category includes refugees and others who have been granted asylum. Those immigrants can eventually apply for permanent residence and citizenship after meeting additional requirements.

The fourth includes people with other immigration protections or documentation, including those with Temporary Protected Status, recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals and certain victims of crimes who qualify for special visas.

TPS provides temporary protection from deportation and allows eligible recipients to work legally in the United States. But the status is temporary by design and does not independently provide a path to permanent residence or citizenship.

For people seeking permanent immigration through the traditional visa system, the process generally starts with a petition.

In most family-based cases, the person seeking to immigrate cannot petition for themselves. A qualifying U.S. citizen family member such as a spouse, parent, child or, in limited circumstances, sibling must file the petition.

Congress limits the number of immigrant visas available in many categories, although spouses and unmarried children under 21 of U.S. citizens are generally exempt from those numerical limits.

Employment-based immigration requires an employer to demonstrate that a position remains available and that the prospective immigrant continues to meet the qualifications for the job.

Applicants also must establish that they are not legally inadmissible to the United States.

That can involve certain criminal offenses, previous immigration violations, public health concerns or, in some circumstances, a determination that the person could become a public charge.

If an immigrant visa is approved, the applicant uses it to enter the United States. Once admitted, the person becomes a lawful permanent resident. The physical green card arrives later.

“The actual green card, as we call it, will come in the mail later,” Meyer said. “But you are a lawful permanent resident once you enter on an immigrant visa.”

Only after obtaining lawful permanent residence does the citizenship clock generally start ticking.

Most permanent residents must wait five years before applying for naturalization. Certain spouses of U.S. citizens can apply after three years if they remain married to and living with their U.S. citizen spouse.

Applicants must also demonstrate basic English proficiency, pass a U.S. history and civics test, establish good moral character and agree to take an oath of allegiance.

Becoming a citizen without authorization

For immigrants who entered the country without authorization, however, the path can be significantly more difficult.

Meyer said federal law generally requires a person seeking permanent residence to have been “inspected and admitted or paroled” into the United States.

That means marriage to a U.S. citizen or having U.S. citizen children does not, by itself, make someone eligible for permanent residence if that person entered the country without permission.

In many cases, the person may have to leave the United States and apply for an immigrant visa through a U.S. consulate abroad, potentially creating additional immigration complications. The Trump administration has enforced this requirement more than other presidents.

People facing deportation can face an even higher legal hurdle.

One form of relief requires an applicant to demonstrate good moral character for 10 years and prove that deportation would cause “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” to certain qualifying relatives.

Meyer said courts have interpreted that requirement as demanding hardship far beyond the ordinary suffering a family would experience from separation.

The complexity of the system also extends beyond the statutes Congress passes.

Federal agencies such as the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice can issue regulations explaining how they will interpret and enforce immigration laws. As a result, the practical application of immigration law can change significantly from one administration to another.

“You get some wide differences between how different administrations will interpret” the law, Meyer said.

For TPS recipients, those changing interpretations can have profound consequences. A person may have lived and worked legally in the United States for years while remaining only temporarily protected from deportation.

The Supreme Court’s recent ruling involving Haitian and Syrian nationals illustrates the stakes. The decision gives the Trump administration greater authority to end certain humanitarian protections and could leave people who have established lives in the United States facing the possibility of removal.

For those immigrants, the question is not necessarily how to become an American citizen.

It may first be whether they have a legal path to remain in the country long enough to become one.

text:
About 50 protesters carrying decorated signs and umbrellas marched toward an immigration detention facility in Conroe two weeks ago. “Show me what community looks like!” they chanted. “This is what community looks like!”

They were headed toward the Montgomery ICE Processing Center to demand the release of two witnesses in the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston. The demonstration was one of several held in the Houston area since Salgado’s July 7 death.

The protesters made themselves heard along the busy highway, where some passing drivers honked in support. But the protest organizer acknowledged that the crowd was relatively small, especially for a shooting that garnered nationwide attention.

U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, who has called for a full investigation into the ICE shooting, said low turnout at Houston-area ICE protests in the weeks since Salgado was killed has disappointed her.

Add Preferred Source

“I just feel like the whole Houston community didn't really come together as Minneapolis and Chicago and LA,” she said in an interview with the Houston Chronicle’s editorial board on Aug. 5.

More than a month after Salgado’s death, some community leaders are reevaluating how they organize, looking for ways to draw larger crowds to protests and turn public outrage into sustained calls for reform. They pointed to several barriers: fear of ICE surveillance and retaliation, limited transportation, divisions among advocacy groups and conservative, statewide leadership that restricts some protests.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

ICE shootings in Los Angeles, Chicago and the Twin Cities have drawn far wider public outrage in the streets, with thousands attending rallies to protest the violence. Organizers in those communities have been able to rely on labor and immigrant-rights networks built over decades, while Houston is still developing much of that infrastructure now.

“Unfortunately, it's not enough. It's not enough for what we're fighting for, and I do believe that it's going to take all of us to work together,” said Frida Adame, founder of We The Lucha, a grassroots organization that launched immediately after the shooting.

Houston has rallied before. Why not now?

Houston is no stranger to mass protests. Thousands rallied after the Moody Park Riot of 1978, while more recent demonstrations have packed streets around City Hall over George Floyd’s killing, the 2017 Women's March , and most recently for No Kings demonstrations against President Donald Trump.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

That history has made the smaller turnout at protests over Salgado’s killing more striking. In Minneapolis, neighbors responded to enforcement beyond street protests, building rapid response hotlines, monitoring ICE activity from their cars and turning local businesses into organizing hubs after the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

“ I was very sad,” Adame said, recalling the first vigil held for Salgado and his family. “It was mixed feelings because I was happy to see that there were people there, but it was sad to see how there was not a lot of people just comparing it to what we've seen in other states.”

That contrast has left Garcia, D-Houston, and other advocates questioning whether Salgado’s race or immigration status played a role in the shooting’s failure to spark broader outrage locally and nationally. The muted response is particularly striking in Houston, where Census data shows foreign-born residents make up about 29% of the population, more than twice the 14% share in Minneapolis.

WHAT SALGADO'S FAMILY SAID: 'I recognized him immediately': Son recounts frantic search for father killed in Houston ICE shooting

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“There hasn't been the outrage for the Salgado killing and the Maine killing like the way there was for two, to be blunt, white citizens,” Garcia said.

Garcia said the community’s response to the killing of U.S. Army soldier and Houston native Vanessa Guillen in 2020 reflected Houston’s diversity. That’s not the case now, she said.

“There was a huge rally at our City Hall with thousands of thousands of people,” she said. “But this time, it just seems like it's been very, very Latino at most of the vigils.”

She has also pointed to divisions among local immigrant rights groups, saying organizations often held separate rallies instead of pooling joint efforts. Adame acknowledged those tensions.

“How can we as organizers ask people to unite if we among organizations can't even get along?” she said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Still, Adame said those tensions have started to ease, with leaders putting aside questions over who should lead and uniting behind the same goal: keeping ICE out of Houston.

“ We had maybe, like, 28 organizations that joined in the same fight,” she said, recalling one of the first joint protests organized after Salgado’s vigil. “It was very beautiful to see because there were many organizations there, some that don't necessarily work with one another.”

Fear of ICE shapes who shows up

Even as groups have begun working closely together, fear continues to keep some people away.

Norma Gonzalez, an organizer with immigrant-rights group Woori Juntos, said some immigrants worry that attending a protest could put them at risk of surveillance — or worse, deportation.

“ I feel like everything that has happened before in Minnesota, it was a warning to all of us to not stand up, to not be with one another,” she said. “They're afraid that if they show up somewhere, someone is going to come after them, most likely ICE.”

While Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz generally supported protesters in his state after Pretti and Good were killed, Texas’ Republican leadership has opposed recent ICE protests.

In 2025, the Texas Legislature passed a bill limiting how students can protest on some university campuses. In 2024, the city of Houston under Mayor John Whitmire tried to limit protests in residential areas, a response to pro-Palestinian activists who held rallies near his home and the homes of other public officials.

The city also lacks sanctuary policies found in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis that limit how local law enforcement and other city employees assist federal immigration enforcement.

“We are in a red state, and we don't have support from the government — at many levels — to be able to do things,” said Cesar Espinosa, the co-founder and executive director of FIEL Houston, a civil rights organization.

Espinosa and FIEL have led the immigrant community’s efforts to end the Houston Police Department’s cooperation with ICE. Espinosa said FIEL organizes activities in a way that minimizes interaction with local and federal law enforcement, but the fear of immigration enforcement is ever-present.

READ MORE:New report reveals how often Houston police turned people over to ICE

“It's not to say that ICE couldn't show up or that we couldn't have a run-in with the police, but we try to mitigate that by trying to be as well organized as possible,” he said. “But the perception that protesting could be very dangerous has hurt in terms of turnout.”

Houston’s size makes protesting harder

Fear isn’t the only barrier organizers point to. Simply getting to a protest can be difficult in a city as sprawling as Houston. Gonzalez explained that traffic, limited public transportation, and parking can all hinder residents from attending.

“There's also very little parking anywhere,” she said. “Sometimes people will want to go to an event, get there, and leave because they can't find where to park.”

Katy Murdza, a senior organizer with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center and Houston Leads, said that some immigrants who have access to a car are also limiting how often they drive because of fear of law enforcement. The Chronicle reported that Houston police officers spent nearly six times longer, on average, on traffic stops involving ICE than on other stops after President Donald Trump took office last year.

DID THE CITY COOPERATE?: Houston vowed to curb ICE cooperation. Police still waited hours for agents.

“ Even people who could drive are now limiting driving as much as possible because of the risk,” Murdza said.

Espinosa said Houston’s size is another deterrent.

“People have to make a decision to spend — if they have limited time — three hours (at a protest) and then about half an hour to an hour in traffic,” he said.

Despite the challenges, Espinosa sees momentum building. He favors more gatherings, no matter the size, and says he welcomes any group that wants to advocate for a cause.

“I think we do the best with what we have. At the end of the day, I've been very clear in telling everybody we should be doing more,” he said. “If there are six events in one day, that’s better. I don't think anybody should try to monopolize what happens with any given issue.”

Part of his optimism stems from younger Houstonians becoming more engaged.

“We had a march in Montrose, and I asked a young lady why she had two flags. She had a Mexican and a Salvadorian flag,” he said. “She said, ‘(my parents) can't come to this, but I'm a U.S. citizen and I can. So, I'm literally carrying my parents on my back.’ I thought that was a really deep and very emotional response.”

Community leaders also see the demonstrations as a way to bring new protesters into the movement.

At the Conroe protest, a young woman marched alongside her mother. They both carried umbrellas they had decorated. One read “ICE OUT,” and the other said “Justicia por Lorenzo” in blue and red marker.

It was the daughter’s first protest.

title: Immigrants today deserve the same Iowa welcome as in past | Opinion
description:
Alexa Lara, a board member for Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, lives in Des Moines.
But for so many Iowa families, immigration is not an abstract debate; It is a lived reality.
But too many immigrant and refugee families today are not met with that same welcome.
Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, for which I am a board member, believes migration is a fundamental human right.
Alexa Lara, a board member for Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, lives in Des Moines.
text:
Alexa Lara, a board member for Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, lives in Des Moines.

Immigration is not a side note in Iowa’s history. It shapes who we are today. For generations, immigrant and refugee families have helped our communities grow, filled essential jobs, started businesses, strengthened local economies, and built lives here rooted in faith, family, hard work and hope.

Immigration is often a political talking point and is the epicenter of political campaigns this election season. But for so many Iowa families, immigration is not an abstract debate; It is a lived reality. It is the story of parents seeking safety for their children, workers filling jobs in struggling rural communities, children growing up in Iowa schools, and families doing what families have always done: trying to build a better future for the next generation.

That is why Republican nominee for governor Zach Lahn’s recent media campaign, which highlights his family’s immigration story, deserves more than a passing mention. He’s claiming his family’s story as a part of Iowa’s story too. We also need to be having a more honest conversation about whether today’s immigrant and refugee families are being offered the same dignity, opportunity and welcome that earlier generations were able to claim.

Almost all of our families have an immigration story. Whether that story began generations ago or just a few years ago, the reasons people come to Iowa remain deeply familiar: safety, family, work, education, and the chance to belong. Those were the reasons my parents immigrated here more than 25 years ago. In Iowa, they found employment, secure housing, strong public schools, and a supportive community where they could raise five children. Their dreams took root here, and today they are proud grandparents to second-generation Iowans.

But too many immigrant and refugee families today are not met with that same welcome. Instead, they face escalating harassment, fear, detention and enforcement tactics that destabilize families and communities. When parents are afraid to go to work, when children fear coming home to an empty house, and when neighbors are treated as threats rather than as people, the harm does not stop at one family’s doorstep. It ripples through classrooms, workplaces, churches, neighborhoods, and local economies.

Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, for which I am a board member, believes migration is a fundamental human right. We also believe Iowa can choose a better path: one that recognizes immigrant families not as political targets, but as valued neighbors, workers, students, business owners, caregivers and community members. We look forward to working with all elected leaders who are willing to support fair, humane and practical immigration policies that strengthen Iowa for everyone.

Iowa’s future will not be stronger if we allow fear to replace fairness or cruelty to replace compassion. Today’s immigrant and refugee families deserve a chance just like previous generations: to live safely, contribute fully, raise their children, and help build a better Iowa for all. As voters, neighbors and leaders, we must decide what kind of state we want to be. Iowa can continue to turn people away, or it can live up to its best traditions by choosing welcome, dignity and justice.

Alexa Lara, a board member for Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, lives in Des Moines.

text:
Blerim Skoro, a 55-year-old Kosovan-born man who says he worked with the CIA on counterterrorism efforts against al-Qaeda and ISIS, has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

An ICE spokesperson told Newsweek that he was arrested on August 3 in Newark, New Jersey, and remains “in ICE custody pending removal from the United States.”

“I worked for the CIA and did all these things for this nation and now I’m here,” Skoro told British newspaper The Times from an ICE detention facility. He added that he was detained while renewing his immigration paperwork, “I went to the office for my scheduled appointment, I handed them my work permit and driver’s license and suddenly they were handcuffing me. It makes no sense.”

Read More on News

His attorneys argue that he helped American national security interests and that a prior immigration ruling requires a judge's permission ahead of deportation, while immigration authorities say the case stems from longstanding legal issues related to his immigration status.

President Donald Trump has pledged to launch the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history. The administration's enforcement efforts have led to the detention of immigrants across a range of legal statuses, including some valid green card holders and visa holders, prompting legal challenges and criticism from immigration advocates.

Newsweek has reported on dozens of cases involving people who were detained after attending appointments at ICE offices, including visits to renew paperwork or complete immigration-related interviews. Administration officials have said the enforcement efforts are necessary to uphold immigration laws, arguing that previous administrations did not enforce them properly.

Newsweek has reached out to Skoro’s legal team for comment via email on Friday. Newsweek filled out a contact request form with the CIA and reached out to the respondent’s legal team via email on Saturday.

Who Is Blerim Skoro?

Skoro was born in the former Yugoslavia and lives in Staten Island, New York, with his American wife, working as a cab driver, per CBS News. He has three children. He first came to the U.S. in 1994 claiming asylum after leaving the Yugoslav Army, The Times reported.

His ties to the U.S. government date back more than two decades when a legal case led to his cooperation with federal authorities and later work with the CIA.

He was arrested in 2000 on federal drug charges. According to the court docket reviewed by Newsweek, he was ordered detention for violating 21 USC 952, for “knowingly and intentionally” conspiring to import heroin to the United States.

The New York Times reported that “he transported at least 14 kilograms of heroin and cocaine and laundered about $670,000 in drug proceeds.”

The prosecutors recommended leniency for him and noted that he provided intelligence about the city’s drug traffickers. Court documents from 2002 state that “Skoro began cooperating with the government immediately. His assistance resulted in the arrest and prosecution of several people involved in an international drug-trafficking organization.”

An ICE spokesperson told Newsweek that following his conviction, “ICE lodged a detainer against Skoro while he was serving time at a federal prison in Allenwood, Pennsylvania.”

He was sentenced to seven years, and shortly into his term he was recruited by U.S. agencies following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. While incarcerated at the federal prison, he says he provided the FBI with information on other cellmates, alleged terrorists, and jihad networks.

He says after his stint as an informant, he was promised U.S. residency. In 2007, he was deported to Kosovo and continued to work for U.S. agencies while traveling around the region in various operations.

“An immigration judge (IJ) ordered SKORO removed from the United States on July 16, 2007, and he was subsequently removed. He illegally reentered the U.S. at an unknown date and location—a felony,” an ICE spokesperson told Newsweek. In 2014, he crossed the U.S.-Canada border to join his family, CBS News reported.

He was arrested in 2016 by immigration agents after using his daughter’s discounted Metro Card in the New York City subway, which led to six months in federal detention and a lengthy immigration battle, the New York Times reported.

In 2022, he was granted a deferral of removal due to the danger and risk to him if he was to go back to Kosovo under the Convention Against Torture. The ruling means he can be sent to another third country, but not Kosovo.

An ICE spokesperson told Newsweek that “an immigration judge in New York, NY found he has no right to remain in the country and ordered Skoro removed again.”

Work With U.S. Intelligence Agencies

Skoro worked for U.S. intelligence agencies for nearly a decade, he told The Times.

His work took him across the Middle East and the Balkans, where he served as an informant and, at one point, allegedly infiltrated al-Qaeda training camps in Pakistan. He said intelligence he provided helped disrupt efforts by al-Qaeda to supply weapons to jihadist groups, uncover financing networks and thwart planned attacks linked to ISIS.

After leaving the U.S., he says he spent two years working undercover for the CIA from 2007-2009, seeking to infiltrate al-Qaida and ISIS networks, according to CBS News. Footage showing him alongside armed militants was later featured in the 2024 documentary The Accidental Spy.

Detention and Court Filings

"I never thought they were going to betray me like this,” Skoro said about the U.S. government in a call with CBS News from detention. He is being held in the Elizabeth Detention Center in New Jersey.

“What message does this send to people thinking of working with the CIA? It shows you will not be protected; you will not be looked after or given safe haven. I was betrayed,” he told The Times.

His attorneys filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on August 4, shortly after his arrest, challenging the legality of his detention.

The filing states that Skoro "worked for the CIA, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the United States Drug Enforcement Agency over the course of nearly a decade," and claims he performed "devoted and heroic work as a United States law enforcement agent,” CBS News reported.

The government has responded to the petition, however, the documents are sealed.

The use of federal habeas corpus petitions has surged during Trump's second term as immigration attorneys increasingly challenge the legality of ICE detentions in federal court.

According to an analysis by ProPublica, immigration attorneys have filed more than 71,000 habeas petitions challenging their clients' detention since January 2025—more than were filed during the previous three presidential administrations combined, including Trump's first.

text:
Representative Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, is criticizing the Trump administration's deportation efforts, telling Newsweek that officials have gone after people who "make zero sense to deport" and arguing some removals lack "common sense and humanity."

Bacon made the remarks while calling attention to the case of Mariana, an Omaha woman who is scheduled to report for removal from the United States on September 18 despite having no criminal record and years of ties to the community.

"The Administration has overreached on deportations, going after people who make zero sense to deport, like Mariana," Bacon told Newsweek in an email. "But I hold Congress most responsible because the laws need improvements. The problem is that too many in Congress are afraid of their shadows on this particular issue."

Read More on News

The comments represent a notable criticism of the administration's immigration enforcement from a Republican lawmaker who has supported securing the U.S. border and removing immigrants who pose public-safety threats.

Earlier Saturday, Bacon shared an opinion piece he wrote for the Omaha World-Herald focused on Mariana's case and posted on X that while deporting dangerous criminals and others who threaten public safety is a "wise and popular" policy, the government has crossed into "inhumane, indecent, & Un-Christian actions" in some cases.

"America must be better than this," Bacon wrote in his X post.

The White House, however, rejected Bacon's criticism.

"We are enforcing the laws passed by Congress. The Trump administration does not pick and choose which laws to enforce," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Newsweek on Saturday. "We encourage illegal aliens to use the CBP Home app to take control of their departure, receive a $2,600 check, and a free flight home."

Bacon's remarks come as the administration continues to expand immigration enforcement efforts. In July, border czar Tom Homan said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) was on pace for a second consecutive record-breaking month for arrests and described the campaign as "deportation-maxxing."

President Donald Trump has pledged to launch the largest mass deportation operation in U.S. history, and immigrants residing in the country both illegally and legally, with valid documentation such as green cards and visas, have been detained. Newsweek has reported dozens of cases involving green card holders and applicants who were swept up in the immigration raids and various arrests.

Newsweek also reached out to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE for comment.

Why Bacon Is Speaking Out

In his Omaha World-Herald op-ed, Bacon described Mariana as an honors graduate and aspiring commercial pilot who came to the U.S. when she was 16 years old after what he called a difficult childhood marked by trauma and instability.

According to the congressman, Mariana taught herself English, graduated from Omaha Central High School, earned an aviation degree from the University of Nebraska Omaha with academic honors and obtained a private pilot's license while supporting herself through work.

Bacon said a removal order was entered after Mariana missed an immigration hearing while she was still a minor. According to Bacon, Mariana has complied with immigration authorities' requirements, including annual check-ins, and previously received stays of removal.

"I have talked to the Secretary of Homeland Security," Bacon told Newsweek. "Because she missed her appointment when she was in [high school] and was abandoned by her parents, the courts ruled against her. She was never personally notified of the hearing."

The congressman argued that deporting people who have built lives in the U.S. and complied with immigration requirements does little to improve public safety.

Deportations That Lack 'Common Sense and Humanity'

Bacon suggested Mariana's situation is not unique, telling Newsweek: “We have a dozen of cases of people in the process of being deported in which most Americans would think lacks common sense and humanity.”

He also expanded his criticism beyond Mariana's case, arguing that some individuals with Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, should be allowed to remain in the U.S. permanently under certain conditions.

"The deportations of TPS folks are also a travesty," Bacon said. "We have people here legally for 10 years, working and many are married to Americans. They should get a pathway to permanent residence if they have a clean record and are working."

TPS allows nationals of designated countries affected by war, natural disasters or other extraordinary conditions to live and work legally in the country temporarily.

The congressman's comments come as ICE detention statistics that were published last month show an increase in immigration enforcement activity. The agency released the updated detention data after a three-month gap in public reporting, showing arrests and detention levels continuing to rise.

ICE was holding 65,765 people in detention as of July 11, up from about 60,300 in early April and approaching the record level of more than 70,700 detainees reported earlier this year, per the data.

Arrests averaged roughly 1,474 per day during the first 11 days of July, exceeding June's average of more than 1,300 daily arrests and marking the highest pace of the current Trump administration, according to an analysis by Syracuse University researcher Austin Kocher.

The same data show approximately 1,246 removals per day between April and July, while the detained population has continued to grow. Researchers analyzing the figures noted that people with no criminal history represent the largest single group currently held in ICE detention.

The share of detainees held solely on immigration violations has increased since April, while the proportion with criminal charges or convictions has declined. Immigration judges have also ordered thousands of detainees released since January, including more than 2,000 releases in May alone.

Bacon's Immigration Reform Push

Bacon's remarks highlight a continuing divide among Republicans over what immigration enforcement should look like after years of political battles over the southern border.

Like many Republicans, Bacon supports stricter border security and has argued the federal government failed for years to adequately enforce immigration laws. Bacon, who is not seeking reelection, has also backed broader immigration reforms that would provide legal protections for some long-term undocumented immigrants.

He pointed to the Dignity Act, legislation he supports, as one possible solution.

"I support the Dignity Act that provides fixes to all this," Bacon told Newsweek.

The proposal would combine enhanced border security measures with legal status opportunities for some immigrants already living in the country.

Bacon argued in his op-ed that Congress has failed for decades to modernize immigration laws, leaving administrations of both parties to rely on temporary policies and shifting enforcement priorities.

What Happens Next

Mariana is currently scheduled to report for removal on September 18, according to Bacon.

The congressman said his office has exhausted available casework options on her behalf and used her situation as an example of what he believes are broader shortcomings in the immigration system.

text:
A federal judge ruled that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority by suspending immigrant visas based on applicants' nationality.

A federal judge has struck down the Trump administration's policy freezing immigrant visa processing for applicants from 75 countries, including several nations with large Black populations. The ruling reverses a major piece of the administration's immigration crackdown after TheGrio reported on the January freeze affecting countries including Nigeria, Jamaica, Haiti, Ethiopia and Somalia, as well as a separate H-1B fee ruling against Trump's $100,000 visa fee.

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas in Manhattan ruled Friday that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his legal authority by suspending immigrant visa issuance based on applicants' nationality. According to Reuters, Vargas called the policy "patently unlawful," finding that federal immigration law does not authorize him to categorically direct consular officers to stop processing immigrant visas.

The suspension took effect in January and covered countries across Africa, the Caribbean, Latin America, the Middle East, the Balkans and South Asia. Among the affected countries were Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Bosnia, Albania, Pakistan and Bangladesh, along with numerous African and Caribbean nations.

The State Department had argued that applicants from the 75 countries faced a high risk of becoming a "public charge" and relying on local, state or federal government resources in the United States.

The lawsuit challenging the policy was brought by Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together, along with immigrant visa applicants and U.S. citizens sponsoring relatives from the affected countries.

Vargas said the blanket restriction conflicted with the immigration system established by Congress because it blocked immigrant visa processing solely on nationality. The State Department did not immediately comment on the ruling.

President Donald Trump has defended his administration's broader immigration crackdown as necessary for domestic security. Rights groups have challenged several administration policies in court, citing concerns including due process, free speech and racial profiling.

text:
A federal judge has struck down a Trump administration ban on issuing immigrant visas to people from 75 countries, saying the policy violated federal immigration law by discriminating on the basis of nationality.

The State Department said earlier this year that it was halting immigrant visas for citizens of Afghanistan, Brazil, Yemen and dozens of other countries because the Trump administration determined people from those nations were likely to need public assistance if they came to the United States.

The policy would have barred the U.S. government from issuing immigrant visas even in cases where consular officers individually assessed applicants and determined they were likely to be self-sufficient in the U.S., according to a ruling Friday by District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas in the Southern District of New York.

"In many ways, this is not a challenging case," Vargas wrote. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 prohibits discrimination on the basis of nationality in the issuance of immigrant visas, Vargas said. However, the Trump administration's policy banned certain people from receiving immigrant visas "based solely on their nationality," the judge wrote.

Vargas cited a U.S. diplomatic cable that instructed consulates to refuse immigrant visas to applicants who had already been approved but whose printed visas hadn't left the consulate.

Vargas said the Trump administration's policy was "contrary to law" and exceeded the authority of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The judge's ruling vacated the visa ban and also set aside visa denials that were based only on the policy.

A State Department spokesperson told NPR the Trump administration is "protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants," adding that the administration doesn't comment on ongoing litigation. When the State Department issued the ban, it said the policy would "remain active until the U.S. can ensure that new immigrants will not extract wealth from the American people."

The ban was part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to limit legal and illegal immigration. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional right to birthright citizenship, rejecting an executive order Trump signed that tried to bar citizenship for babies born in the U.S. to parents who either entered the country illegally or who are living and working here legally with temporary visas. The executive order never went into effect because lower court judges ruled it was unconstitutional.

Susan Welber, supervising attorney at The Legal Aid Society, which represented plaintiffs in the lawsuit against the federal government, says the 75-country visa ban was "premised on a fiction" that residents of the targeted nations are likely to use public resources if they come to the U.S.

"Any time that we can fight back against policies that are based on fictions and untruths and prejudices, I think we're making for a more just immigration system," Welber says.

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit included the Catholic Immigration Legal Network and African Communities Together, which provide immigration legal services, as well as six U.S. citizens who filed family-based immigration petitions on behalf of relatives and five "intending immigrants" who filed employment-based petitions on their own behalf.

"The suspension of lawful visa processing across 75 countries separated spouses, parents, and children who were simply following the legal immigration process," Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, said in a statement.

Plaintiffs' lawyers said Friday's ruling will allow their clients to proceed through the immigration process.

"For 75 countries' worth of families, this decision means a return to fair, case-by-case review, and a chance to be reunited with their loved ones," said Antionette Dozier, senior attorney for Western Center on Law & Poverty, which represented the Catholic Legal Immigration Network. "No administration gets to override the law because it deems an applicant's nationality unacceptable."

text:
A federal judge in New York has vacated a Trump administration policy that suspended the processing of visas from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, whose nationals the Trump administration deemed likely to require public assistance in the United States.

U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, set aside the policy Friday as “contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority by issuing the policy, which “runs afoul” of the Immigration and Nationality Act by mandating "the refusal of visas to eligible applicants without any basis in law,” the judge ruled.

Judge says power lies with consular officers

Vargas said the policy also undermines the congressional requirement that puts consular officers at the forefront of any visa decision. “Congress imbued these officers with exclusive authority and discretion to determine if an immigrant is eligible for a visa based upon review of specific and detailed criteria set forth in the statute,” she wrote. “The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme."

The policy was challenged by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals, including six whose family members had been refused visas. The remaining five are outside the country and had filed “employment-based petitions” to come to the United States.

Advocates say keeping families apart is cruel

“We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together,” said Anna Gallagher, the executive director of CLINIC, a national nonprofit that provides training, resources, and support to a network of immigration legal service providers and was one of the plaintiffs.

Local

“Catholic social teaching calls us to uphold the dignity of every person and recognize the family as the foundation of society,” she said in a statement. “This decision affirms both those values and the rule of law, allowing families to once again move forward toward reunification.”

Another plaintiff is African Communities Together, a Harlem-based nonprofit. One of its leaders called the ruling “a tremendous victory for the rule of law." “This unlawful and racist ban caused immeasurable harm, cruelly keeping families and loved ones apart,” Diana Konate, deputy executive director for policy and advocacy, said in a statement. “Today, we are elated to tell our community members: this ban is no more.”

Trump expands his anti-immigration agenda

President Donald Trump has imposed a growing list of immigration and travel bans mostly for people from Africa, Asia and Latin America. The State Department said Saturday that the Trump administration is “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants,” and that it would not comment on pending litigation.

At the time the policy was issued, the State Department said it had instructed consular officers to halt immigrant visa applications from the 75 countries in accordance with a broader order in November that tightened rules around potential immigrants who might become “public charges.” Relying on Council of Economic Advisers data, the State Department said that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from these countries received some form of public assistance.

A separate notice sent to all U.S. embassies and consulates said that non-immigrant visa applicants also should be “fully vetted and screened” for the possibility that they might seek public benefits in the United States.

The cable, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, noted several times that the applicant must prove they won't apply for public benefits while in the U.S., and that consular officers who suspect the applicant might apply should require them to fill out a form proving their financial bona fides.

The ruling is the latest example of the courts upending Trump’s immigration agenda. In June, a federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that made it harder for immigrants from dozens of countries to enter and stay in America — affecting elements like asylum, work permits, green cards, and citizenship applications. That judge said the policy threw countless immigrants’ lives “into indeterminate legal limbo,” and accused the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of ignoring the law.

text:
The end of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for more than 55,000 Hondurans living in the United States is raising concern in Honduras, where the number of people returning from the United States has already increased significantly this year.

The Honduran government confirmed that TPS will end, but officials have sought to reassure the public that the decision does not necessarily mean an immediate mass return of Honduran migrants or an abrupt decline in remittances.

At the same time, human rights and migrant-support organizations are warning that Honduras must prepare for the possibility of more people returning—many after spending decades building their lives in the United States.

The concern comes as Honduras is already experiencing a substantial increase in return migration. From January 1 through August 14, 45,632 Hondurans had returned to the country, compared with 36,216 during the same period in 2025. According to figures analyzed by Honduras’ National Human Rights Commissioner (Conadeh), that represents a 26% increase.

The United States accounts for the overwhelming majority of these returns. Approximately 40,717 people, or 89.2% of all returnees this year, came from the United States—a 47.3% increase compared with the 27,628 Hondurans who returned from the U.S. during the same period last year.

Those numbers have intensified concerns about what could happen as TPS protections disappear.

For Many, Returning Means Starting Over

Elsy Reyes, coordinator of Conadeh’s Human Mobility Ombudsman’s Office, said the growing number of returnees is concerning because many will need support rebuilding their economic and social lives in Honduras.

“We are seeing that around 89% come from the United States,” Reyes said, warning that Honduras needs to prepare for a potentially larger population of deported migrants by the end of the year.

For some returnees, going back to Honduras means returning to a country they barely recognize. A significant number have lived in the United States for 20 years or more. They may have homes, families, jobs, friendships, and entire communities there, while their connections and economic opportunities in Honduras may have weakened over time.

The demographic profile of those already returning underscores the challenge. Of the 45,632 returnees recorded this year, 30,919 are men, 7,172 are women, 2,722 are girls, and 4,818 are boys. About 76% are between the ages of 21 and 50, placing them primarily within the working-age population.

For Conadeh, the challenge is not simply helping people cross the border and arrive safely. It is helping them rebuild a life.

Reyes estimates that more than 80% of returnees need some form of economic assistance to find work and establish a livelihood. Without employment and other forms of support, she warned, some may once again see migration as their only viable option.

Mercedes Pérez of the Mennonite Social Action Commission (CASM) said the situation is further complicated by Honduras’ climate challenges, which are already making it difficult for many people to maintain their livelihoods.

She called for the government to declare a migration emergency and develop short-, medium-, and long-term plans—not only for Hondurans who may return following the end of TPS, but also for the people already arriving every day.

Honduras currently receives approximately three flights carrying returnees each day, in addition to people who return voluntarily or arrive by land after spending time in Mexico.

For organizations working with migrants, the question is therefore larger than how many people will return. It is whether Honduras will have enough jobs, housing, healthcare, psychological support, and economic opportunities to help them rebuild their lives.

What the End of TPS Means

The Honduran government says the end of TPS is real and will have consequences, but emphasizes that it does not automatically mean that all TPS beneficiaries must leave the United States immediately.

Foreign Minister Mireya Agüero acknowledged that for people who depended exclusively on TPS to remain in the country and maintain employment authorization, its termination represents a significant loss of protection; yet she stressed, “The loss of TPS does not, by itself, imply an immediate return.”

Each person’s situation will depend on factors including how long they have lived in the United States, their family and community ties, possible alternative avenues for legal status, and whether they have pending legal proceedings.

The TPS termination itself follows a lengthy legal and political process. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services confirmed the cancellation of TPS for Honduras in September 2025, after which the decision became the subject of legal challenges. Agüero said U.S. Supreme Court decisions issued in June 2026 involving Haiti and Syria have narrowed the possibilities for judicial review of TPS decisions, while another ruling involving Ethiopia was announced this week.

Honduras Seeks More Time

Rather than preparing only for a mass return, the Honduran government says it is pursuing diplomatic measures aimed at creating a more gradual transition.

President Nasry “Tito” Asfura sent a letter on June 30 to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio requesting an “additional, reasonable, and clearly defined period of orderly transition.”

Honduras is also asking for the temporary continuation of employment authorization and for expanded access to employment-based visas for Hondurans affected by the end of TPS.

TPS was granted to Hondurans in 1999 following Hurricane Mitch, which devastated Central America in late 1998, killing thousands and causing enormous destruction in Honduras.

Agüero said the Honduran government is approaching the issue “seriously, without creating alarm,” while coordinating a response through the National Council for the Protection of Honduran Migrants (Conaprohm).

The goal, she said, is to ensure a dignified and protected reintegration for those who ultimately return.

For the thousands of Hondurans who have spent years or even decades in the United States, however, the end of TPS represents more than a change in immigration status. It may force difficult decisions about where home is, how to support a family, and how to rebuild a life in a country many left years ago.

And with returns from the United States already up nearly 47% this year, Honduras is being pressed to prepare for that possibility before the full effects of the end of TPS are felt.

Agents from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained an Ecuadorian mother and her teenage daughter this Friday while they were receiving medical attention at a hospital in Florida, where they had arrived minutes earlier after surviving a traffic accident, according to the Ecuadorian media outlet Teleamazonas.

Grace Calero, 39 years old, and her daughter Giulianna Carriel, 19, were traveling on a highway in Florida when another vehicle lost control, veered into their lane, and collided with them, causing their car to overturn. Both were rushed to HCA Florida Poinciana Hospital, where Grace was diagnosed with cervical injuries and given a neck brace, while Giulianna experienced a nervous breakdown due to the emotional impact of the accident.

It was in that emergency room where immigration agents burst in and proceeded to arrest them. Grace's sister, Gia Calero, confirmed that both were receiving medical attention when they were detained.

El momento quedó grabado en un video que se difundió ampliamente: las imágenes muestran a las dos mujeres esposadas y escoltadas fuera del centro médico ante la mirada de pacientes y personal del hospital.

The arrest occurs within the framework of the immigration policy of the Trump administration, which at the end of January 2025 revoked the federal guideline on "sensitive locations," a rule that had prevented ICE from making arrests in hospitals, churches, and schools for decades. Since then, public areas of medical centers—lobbies, hallways, and waiting rooms—can be accessed by immigration agents without a court order.

Florida has become one of the states with the highest intensity of operations: between January 2025 and March 2026, nearly 39,000 arrests were recorded in the state, according to data from the AP agency cited by the broadcaster WLRN. Nationwide, ICE set a record in June 2026 with over 39,500 detentions in a single month, at a rate close to 2,000 arrests per day.

The operations have progressively expanded to new scenarios. In recent weeks, ICE intensified its arrests in airports across the country, raising alarm within migrant communities. A survey published this month revealed a growing public debate over whether the agency is using excessive force in its operations, in a context where the use of force in detention centers increased by 37% during 2025.

The case of Grace Calero and Giulianna Carriel adds to a series of detentions of Ecuadorian citizens by ICE that have garnered media attention in 2026, including that of Chantal Morales, who was released after her arrest. The Ecuadorian community in the United States is among the most affected by the intensification of immigration operations in the past year and a half.

The arrest of a mother with cervical injuries and her daughter in a state of nervous crisis, inside a hospital and in front of the medical staff, has sparked outrage both in Ecuador and among organizations advocating for the rights of migrants.
